lessons.title: Introduction to Comprehension
lessons.summary: An overview of comprehension as a skill, its importance in JAMB, and the various skills tested.

blocks.text: Comprehension is a fundamental skill in the JAMB Use of English examination. It is not merely about reading a passage and finding answers directly stated in the text. True comprehension involves understanding the deeper meaning of the text, the author's intent, the relationships between ideas, and the ability to draw logical conclusions. This lesson introduces you to the core skills you will need for this section.
What is Comprehension?

Comprehension is the ability to understand and interpret written text. It goes beyond just recognizing words; it involves constructing meaning from the information presented. A good reader can identify the main idea, understand supporting details, infer meaning, and analyze the author's tone and purpose.
Why is Comprehension Important in JAMB?

items: A significant portion of the Use of English paper is dedicated to comprehension passages.
It tests your ability to process information quickly and accurately, a vital skill for university studies.
It helps you develop critical thinking and analytical skills.
It often carries a high mark allocation, making it a key area for scoring well.

blocks.text: Core Comprehension Skills You Will Develop

items: Identifying the Main Idea: What is the central point the author is trying to make?
Understanding Supporting Details: What facts, examples, or evidence does the author use to support the main idea?
Making Inferences: What can you deduce from the passage that is not explicitly stated?
Understanding Vocabulary in Context: What does a particular word or phrase mean as used in the passage?
Identifying Tone and Attitude: What is the author's feeling or viewpoint towards the subject? Is it critical, supportive, neutral, humorous?
Determining the Author's Purpose: Why did the author write the passage? To inform, persuade, entertain, or explain?
Understanding Relationships Between Ideas: How are different ideas in the passage connected? (e.g., cause and effect, comparison and contrast, problem and solution)

blocks.text: Approach comprehension passages with an active mind. Ask questions as you read: 'What is this about?', 'What is the author's point?', 'Why is this detail included?'. Active reading is the key to deep understanding.

lessons.title: Identifying the Main Idea
lessons.summary: A guide to finding the central point of a passage, distinguishing it from supporting details.

blocks.text: The main idea is the most important point or central message that the author wants to communicate about a topic. It is the controlling idea of a paragraph or an entire passage. All other sentences in the passage are there to support, explain, or expand on this main idea. Identifying the main idea is essential for summarizing, making inferences, and answering a wide range of comprehension questions.
How to Find the Main Idea

items: Read the entire passage carefully to get a general sense of what it's about.
Ask yourself: 'What is the one thing the author wants me to understand about this topic?'
Look for a topic sentence. This is often the first sentence, but it can also be the last, or in the middle of the paragraph. It clearly states the main point.
If there is no single topic sentence, consider the overall message of all the sentences together. What is the common thread?
Eliminate details that are too specific. The main idea is a general statement that summarizes the entire passage.

blocks.title: Finding the Main Idea in a Paragraph
blocks.text:
Passage:

Nigeria is a land of immense cultural diversity. With over 250 ethnic groups, each with its own unique language, traditions, and art forms, the country is a vibrant mosaic of cultures. From the colorful festivals of the Yoruba in the west to the intricate bronze works of the Igbo in the east, and the rich nomadic traditions of the Fulani in the north, the cultural landscape is incredibly rich. This diversity is a source of national pride and a significant attraction for tourism.

Main Idea: Nigeria is a very culturally diverse country.

Notice how the other sentences provide examples and descriptions that support this central idea.
Main Idea vs. Topic

blocks.caption: Distinguishing Topic from Main Idea
rows: The general subject of the passage.
The specific point the author is making about the topic.
Climate change poses the single greatest threat to global food security.

blocks.text: In JAMB, you will often be asked for the 'best title' for a passage. A good title is like a concise statement of the main idea. It should capture the essence of the passage.
A sentence that expresses the main idea of the paragraph in which it occurs. It is often the first sentence but can also be found elsewhere.
JAMB Focus: Avoiding Distractors

items: Option is too broad: This option might be true but covers a wider area than the specific passage addresses.
Option is too narrow: This option mentions a supporting detail rather than the overall message.
Option is stated incorrectly: This option distorts or contradicts the author's message.
Option is a paraphrase of a detail: It sounds like the passage but is a detail, not the main idea.

blocks.text: Practice Question 1 Read the passage below and select the option that best expresses the main idea. 'The introduction of digital learning platforms in Nigerian universities has been a double-edged sword. On one hand, it has increased access to information and allowed for more flexible learning schedules. Students in remote areas can now connect to lectures and resources that were previously unavailable. On the other hand, the digital divide has become more pronounced, with students from lower-income backgrounds struggling to afford the necessary devices and data. This creates a new form of inequality within the educational system.' A. Digital learning is beneficial for students in remote areas. B. The digital divide is a major problem in Nigeria. C. Digital learning platforms have both positive and negative impacts on Nigerian university education. D. Nigerian students are facing challenges in their studies.

Correct Answer: C Explanation: The passage clearly presents both advantages ('On one hand') and disadvantages ('On the other hand') of digital learning platforms. Option A is a supporting detail, Option B is too broad, and Option D is also too broad and not the specific point of the passage. Option C accurately summarizes the central message.

Practice Question 2 What is the main idea of the following passage? 'Chinua Achebe's novel, Things Fall Apart, is often studied as a seminal work of African literature. It narrates the story of Okonkwo, a powerful Igbo warrior, and the tragic events that befall him and his community with the arrival of European colonialism. Beyond its historical context, the novel delves into timeless themes of tradition versus change, masculinity, and the destructive nature of fear. Achebe's masterful use of Igbo proverbs and storytelling techniques has made it a celebrated literary classic that continues to resonate with readers worldwide.' A. Things Fall Apart is about Igbo traditions. B. Things Fall Apart is an important literary work that explores complex themes and has had a lasting impact. C. Chinua Achebe was a great Nigerian author. D. The arrival of colonialism was a tragic event for the Igbo.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The passage discusses the novel's importance, its themes, and its lasting impact. While A, C, and D might be true, they are either details or related ideas. Option B captures the comprehensive point of the passage.

lessons.title: Understanding Supporting Details
lessons.summary: Learn to identify facts, examples, and other pieces of evidence that support the main idea and answer specific questions.

blocks.text: Supporting details are the specific facts, examples, reasons, statistics, and other pieces of information that the author uses to develop and explain the main idea. If the main idea is the 'skeleton' of the passage, the supporting details are the 'flesh' that gives it life and substance. Comprehending these details is crucial for answering specific questions about the text.
Types of Supporting Details

items: Examples: Specific instances or illustrations of the main idea.
Facts and Statistics: Objective, verifiable information.
Reasons: Explanations that tell 'why' something is the case.
Descriptions: Details that help the reader visualize a person, place, or thing.
Comparisons and Contrasts: Show how things are similar or different.
Testimony or Quotations: Words from experts or other sources to support a point.

blocks.title: Identifying Supporting Details
blocks.text:
Main Idea: Lagos is one of the most congested cities in the world.

Supporting Details:

  • A typical journey that takes 20 minutes at midnight can take up to 3 hours during peak traffic (Fact).
  • The city's road network is overburdened by its rapidly growing population of over 15 million people (Reason).
  • Navigating the streets, one will find an endless stream of cars, 'danfo' buses, and 'okada' motorcycles (Description).
  • This congestion is estimated to cost the Nigerian economy billions of naira annually in lost productivity (Statistic).
How to Approach Questions on Details
Questions on supporting details are often the most straightforward. They require you to locate information that is explicitly stated in the passage.

items: Read the question carefully and note the key terms.
Scan the passage for these key terms or their synonyms.
Read the sentence or sentences containing those terms.
Match the information in the passage to the options provided. The correct option will be a direct paraphrase or a near-direct quote from the text.

blocks.text: JAMB traps often involve changing a single word in a detail to alter its meaning entirely. For example, replacing 'increase' with 'decrease' or 'some' with 'all'. Read every word carefully before selecting an answer.

Practice Question Read the passage and answer the question below. 'The economic impact of the tourism industry in Nigeria is often underestimated. While it is not yet a leading sector like oil, it provides a significant source of employment, particularly in states like Cross River and Edo. Attractions such as the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove and the Obudu Cattle Ranch draw both local and international visitors. A recent government report indicated that the sector contributed 3.2% to the nation's GDP and supported over a million jobs directly and indirectly.' According to the passage, which of the following is a source of employment in the tourism industry? A. The oil industry B. States like Cross River and Edo C. The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove D. The Obudu Cattle Ranch

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The passage explicitly states: 'it provides a significant source of employment, particularly in states like Cross River and Edo.' Option A is incorrect because the oil industry is mentioned as a contrast. Options C and D are specific attractions, not sources of employment themselves, but rather attractions that help generate employment in those states.

lessons.title: Making Inferences
lessons.summary: Learn to 'read between the lines' to understand implied meanings and draw logical conclusions.

blocks.text: Inference is the process of drawing logical conclusions from information that is implied but not directly stated. It is often described as 'reading between the lines.' While main ideas and supporting details are explicit, inferences require you to use your own reasoning and understanding of the world to deduce what the author is suggesting. This is a higher-order skill that is frequently tested in JAMB.
Why Inferences are Important

items: Authors often prefer to suggest or imply ideas rather than state them directly to create a more subtle or powerful effect.
It helps you understand the full meaning of the text.
It is a crucial skill for critical thinking and analysis.

blocks.text: A logical conclusion or deduction based on evidence and reasoning from the text, combined with your own prior knowledge.

blocks.title: Making an Inference
blocks.text:
Statement in a passage: 'Bola's hands were shaking as she stepped onto the podium. Her throat felt tight, and she could barely whisper the first words of her speech. She glanced at her notes, but the words seemed to dance on the page.'

Inference: Bola was extremely nervous.

This is not directly stated, but we can infer it from the evidence: shaking hands, tight throat, difficulty speaking, and inability to read her notes.
How to Make Correct Inferences

items: Read the text carefully and identify the explicit facts and details.
Ask yourself: 'What is the author implying by saying this?' or 'What can I logically conclude based on this information?'
Use your own common sense and experience to connect the dots.
Ensure there is evidence in the text to support your inference. It should be a reasonable deduction, not a wild guess.
Avoid inferences that go beyond the text or have no textual basis.

blocks.caption: Common JAMB Inference Questions
rows: Ability to deduce a hidden meaning.
'The author implies that the government's policy on education will be...'
It can be inferred from the passage that...
Ability to draw a logical conclusion.
'It can be inferred from the passage that the writer believes...'
The tone of the passage suggests that...
'The tone of the passage suggests that the author feels...'

blocks.text: A common mistake is to choose an option that is a factual detail from the passage rather than an inference. The correct answer must be something that is not directly stated, but is logically derived from the text.

Practice Question 1 Read the passage and answer the question. 'The campus was eerily quiet. The usually bustling walkways were empty, and the library, normally a hive of activity, was dark and shuttered. A single notice flapped on the main gate, its message already blurry from the afternoon drizzle.' It can be inferred from the passage that the campus is... A. closed for the day. B. having a holiday. C. empty and mostly abandoned for some reason. D. preparing for a storm.

Correct Answer: C Explanation: The details 'quiet,' 'empty,' 'dark and shuttered,' and 'single notice' all imply that the campus is empty and not functioning. Option C is a safe, logical inference. Options A and B are too specific—it could be closed for a strike, a public holiday, or a vacation. Option D is an unsupported guess; there's no mention of a storm.

Practice Question 2 Read the passage and answer the question. 'The CEO's speech was met with polite applause. As he detailed the company's plan for the next quarter, several board members exchanged knowing glances. One of them, Mrs. Adeyemi, was seen discreetly shaking her head.' What can be inferred about the board members' reaction to the CEO's speech? A. They were all in agreement and supportive. B. They were enthusiastic about the new plan. C. Some of them were skeptical or disapproving of the plan. D. They were not paying attention.

Correct Answer: C Explanation: The 'knowing glances' and Mrs. Adeyemi shaking her head are strong clues that some board members were not fully on board with the plan. The applause was 'polite,' not enthusiastic, further supporting this inference. Option C is the only choice that explains this subtext.

lessons.title: Vocabulary in Context
lessons.summary: Learn to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words by analyzing the surrounding text in the passage.

blocks.text: The 'Vocabulary in Context' questions are a staple of the JAMB Use of English comprehension section. They test your ability to determine the meaning of a word or phrase as it is used in the passage. You are not simply being tested on your knowledge of dictionary definitions; you are being tested on your ability to use context clues to unlock meaning. This skill is vital for independent learning and understanding complex texts.
Strategies for Decoding Vocabulary in Context

items: Look for Definition Clues: The author may directly define the word. Often signalled by words like 'is,' 'means,' 'refers to,' or punctuation like commas and dashes.
Look for Synonym Clues: The author may use a similar word or phrase nearby. Words like 'or,' 'in other words,' 'like,' and 'as' often signal a synonym.
Look for Antonym Clues: The author may contrast the word with its opposite. Words like 'but,' 'although,' 'however,' 'unlike,' and 'on the other hand' can signal an antonym.
Look for Inference Clues: You can infer the meaning from the general sense of the sentence or paragraph. Ask yourself: 'What kind of word would make sense here?'
Analyze the Structure: If you know the meaning of prefixes, suffixes, and root words, you can often guess the meaning of the new word.

blocks.title: Using Context Clues
blocks.text:
Definition Clue: 'The country was in a state of anarchy, a complete absence of government and law.'

Synonym Clue: 'The new policy was ambiguous, or unclear, leading to confusion among the staff.'

Antonym Clue: 'Unlike her loquacious sister who never stops talking, Ada is quite taciturn.'

Inference Clue: 'The sound of the cacophony made it impossible to hear the speaker. Everyone was shouting, horns were honking, and music was blasting from several different stalls.'

Do not rely solely on your prior knowledge of a word. If you know a common definition, but the passage seems to use it differently, always trust the context. JAMB questions often test secondary or less common meanings of common words.

Practice Question 1 Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the underlined word as it is used in the context. 'The manager's decision to remain obdurate in the negotiations, refusing to budge even a little, ultimately led to a breakdown in talks.' A. Flexible B. Stubborn C. Unclear D. Patient
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The phrase 'refusing to budge even a little' acts as a definition clue. This directly describes a stubborn person. Therefore, 'obdurate' means stubborn.

Practice Question 2 Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the underlined word as it is used in the context. 'Despite the paucity of resources, the community health center was able to provide essential services to the villagers.' A. Abundance B. Scarcity C. Quality D. Waste

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The word 'Despite' acts as an antonym clue. If the center was able to provide services 'despite' this situation, it must have been a negative condition. 'Paucity' suggests a lack or scarcity, which is the only fitting option.

Practice Question 3 Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the underlined word as it is used in the context. 'The laconic soldier responded to the general's question with a simple 'Yes, sir.' and did not add any further explanation.' A. Verbose B. Nervous C. Brief D. Disrespectful

Correct Answer: C Explanation: The context clue is that he responded with a 'simple 'Yes, sir'' and gave 'no further explanation.' This describes someone who is brief and uses few words. 'Laconic' means using very few words.

lessons.title: Tone, Attitude, and Purpose
lessons.summary: Learn to identify the author's feeling towards the subject and why they wrote the passage.

blocks.text: Understanding the author's tone, attitude, and purpose is a crucial aspect of advanced comprehension. It requires moving beyond the surface information to analyze the author's perspective. These questions test your ability to 'read between the lines' and understand the subtle messages in a text.
Tone and Attitude

Tone is the author's attitude toward the subject matter. Attitude is often used interchangeably with tone. It is conveyed through the author's word choice, sentence structure, and imagery. It's the emotional quality of the writing.
The writer's attitude or feeling towards the subject of the text. It can be formal, informal, critical, supportive, humorous, sarcastic, serious, etc.

blocks.caption: Common Tones in JAMB Passages
rows: The author points out faults, weaknesses, or problems.
The author is positive, encouraging, or in agreement.
The author presents facts without showing emotion or opinion.
The author uses words that are opposite to their literal meaning to mock or ridicule.
The author is lighthearted, using jokes or amusing descriptions.
The author is formal and grave, discussing important or sad topics.

blocks.text: Author's Purpose
Purpose is the reason why the author wrote the passage. This is often driven by one of the following goals: to inform, to persuade, to entertain, or to explain.
The author's primary reason for writing the text (e.g., to inform, persuade, entertain, or explain).

blocks.title: Identifying Purpose
blocks.text:
• To Inform: A news report about a recent political event. ('The electoral commission has announced the results...')
  • To Persuade: An editorial arguing for a new policy. ('The government must urgently address the issue of inflation...')
  • To Entertain: A short story or a humorous anecdote. ('Chinwe couldn't help but laugh as her dog chased its own tail...')
  • To Explain: A scientific article about photosynthesis. ('Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert sunlight into energy...')
To identify the purpose, ask yourself: 'What is the author trying to achieve with this text?' The answer will usually be a verb like 'persuade,' 'inform,' 'criticize,' 'entertain,' or 'explain.'

Practice Question 1 Read the passage below and identify the author's tone. 'It is truly unfortunate that our leaders have once again failed to keep their promises to the people. They speak eloquently of progress and development, yet the roads remain in disrepair, and the hospitals are understaffed. The ordinary citizen is left to bear the burden of their incompetence and corruption.' A. Neutral B. Sarcastic C. Critical D. Humorous
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The words 'unfortunate,' 'failed,' 'incompetence,' and 'corruption' all point to a strongly negative and critical tone. The author is clearly criticizing the leaders.

Practice Question 2 What is the primary purpose of the passage in Question 1? A. To inform the reader about a new government policy. B. To persuade the reader that the leaders are failing. C. To entertain the reader with a political story. D. To explain how a government works.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The author is not just stating facts; they are using strong language to convince the reader of the leaders' failure. The purpose is to persuade the reader to adopt a certain viewpoint.

lessons.title: Description in Comprehension
lessons.summary: How to identify and analyze descriptive passages, focusing on sensory details and imagery.

blocks.text: A descriptive passage aims to create a vivid picture of a person, place, object, or scene in the reader's mind. It relies heavily on sensory details—sight, sound, smell, touch, and taste—to bring the subject to life. Understanding descriptive passages is important because JAMB may ask you to identify the mood, atmosphere, or dominant impression created by the description.
Features of Descriptive Writing

items: Sensory Language: Use of words that appeal to the senses. (e.g., 'crimson sunset,' 'fragrant flowers,' 'crunchy leaves').
Imagery: Figurative language like similes and metaphors that create mental pictures.
Adjectives and Adverbs: Rich use of descriptive words to modify nouns and verbs.
Specific Details: Focus on concrete, specific details rather than vague generalities.

blocks.title: Example of Descriptive Passage
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The old market was a symphony of sights and sounds. The air was thick with the aroma of frying plantains and spices. Stalls overflowed with colorful fabrics and gleaming pots. The chatter of buyers and sellers created a constant hum, punctuated by the occasional cry of a vendor advertising his wares.'

Analysis: This passage uses sensory details (aroma, colors, sounds) to create a vivid picture of the market. The dominant impression is one of vibrant activity.
How to Answer Questions on Descriptive Passages

items: Identify the dominant impression or mood (e.g., peaceful, chaotic, joyful).
Look for the specific sensory details used and what they contribute.
Recognize the use of figurative language (similes, metaphors) and its effect.

blocks.text: Practice Question Read the following description and identify the dominant impression. 'The room was suffocatingly small. Dusty books were piled high on every surface, and the only light came from a single, dim bulb that flickered nervously. The air was stale and heavy, making each breath feel like a struggle.' A. Cozy and inviting B. Claustrophobic and oppressive C. Bright and cheerful D. Clean and orderly
Correct Answer: B Explanation: Words like 'suffocatingly small,' 'dim bulb,' 'stale and heavy' all contribute to a feeling of claustrophobia and oppression.

lessons.title: Narration in Comprehension
lessons.summary: Understanding narrative passages, including plot, sequence of events, and point of view.

blocks.text: A narrative passage tells a story. It presents a sequence of events, often involving characters, a setting, and a plot. In JAMB comprehension, you may be asked to identify the sequence of events, understand the narrator's point of view, or infer character motivations.
Elements of Narrative Writing

items: Plot: The series of events that make up the story, often including an exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.
Characters: The people (or animals) in the story.
Setting: The time and place where the story occurs.
Point of View: The perspective from which the story is told (e.g., first person, third person).
Chronology: The order of events—often chronological but may include flashbacks.

blocks.title: Narrative Passage Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'Tunde woke up late. He rushed to get dressed, skipping breakfast. As he ran to the bus stop, he realized he had forgotten his wallet. He had to turn back, and by the time he reached the bus stop, the bus had already left. He knew he would be late for his interview.'

Analysis: This is a narrative with a clear sequence of events (waking late, rushing, forgetting wallet, missing bus). The effect is to build tension and show the character's predicament.
Answering Questions on Narrative Passages

items: Pay attention to time markers (e.g., 'then,' 'afterward,' 'before') to follow the sequence.
Identify the narrator's point of view and how it affects the story.
Consider the cause-and-effect relationships between events.

blocks.text: Practice Question Read the narrative and answer the question. 'After the storm had passed, the villagers emerged from their homes to survey the damage. The main road was blocked by fallen trees, and several houses had lost their roofs. The chief immediately called for a meeting to organize the cleanup.' What is the sequence of events in this passage? A. Meeting called, storm passed, villagers emerged, damage surveyed. B. Storm passed, villagers emerged, damage surveyed, meeting called. C. Villagers emerged, storm passed, damage surveyed, meeting called. D. Meeting called, damage surveyed, storm passed, villagers emerged.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The passage states: 'After the storm had passed, the villagers emerged... to survey the damage. The chief immediately called for a meeting.' This is the chronological order.

lessons.title: Exposition in Comprehension
lessons.summary: Recognizing expository passages that explain or inform, focusing on definitions, processes, and facts.

blocks.text: An expository passage is written to explain, inform, or describe a topic objectively. It presents facts, definitions, processes, or cause-and-effect relationships without the author's personal opinion. In JAMB, you may be asked to identify the main idea, the purpose, or the supporting evidence in an expository text.
Features of Expository Writing

items: Objective Tone: The author remains neutral and factual.
Definitions and Explanations: Key terms are defined and concepts are clarified.
Logical Organization: Often organized by cause-effect, comparison-contrast, or problem-solution.
Use of Evidence: Facts, statistics, and examples are used to support claims.

blocks.title: Expository Passage Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy. This process takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells, using chlorophyll to capture sunlight. The plant combines carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen. Oxygen is released as a byproduct, while glucose serves as food for the plant.'

Analysis: This passage explains a scientific process in a clear, factual manner. It defines photosynthesis and describes the steps involved.
Tips for Answering Questions on Expository Passages

items: Look for the main idea—what is being explained?
Identify the organizational pattern (e.g., cause-effect, sequence).
Distinguish between facts and opinions—expository texts are usually factual.

blocks.text: Practice Question Read the passage and answer the question. 'The human circulatory system consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood. The heart pumps blood through a network of arteries, veins, and capillaries. Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, while veins return deoxygenated blood back to the heart. This continuous circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells and removes waste products.' What is the primary purpose of this passage? A. To persuade readers to exercise. B. To explain the structure and function of the circulatory system. C. To describe a personal experience with heart disease. D. To argue for better healthcare.
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The passage provides a factual explanation of the circulatory system, its components, and its function. This is clearly expository.

lessons.title: Argumentation and Persuasion
lessons.summary: Understanding persuasive passages, recognizing arguments, and identifying persuasive techniques.

blocks.text: An argumentative or persuasive passage aims to convince the reader to adopt a certain viewpoint or take a specific action. Unlike expository texts, persuasive texts are not neutral; they present a clear opinion and use reasoning and emotional appeals to sway the reader. JAMB may test your ability to identify the author's argument, the evidence used, and any persuasive techniques.
Key Features of Argumentative Passages

items: Clear Thesis: The author states a clear position (for or against).
Reasons and Evidence: The author provides logical reasons and factual evidence to support the thesis.
Counterarguments: Sometimes the author addresses opposing views to strengthen their own argument.
Persuasive Language: Emotional language, rhetorical questions, and strong adjectives may be used.

blocks.title: Argumentative Passage Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'It is time for the government to implement stricter regulations on single-use plastics. These plastics are a major cause of environmental pollution, clogging our waterways and harming marine life. While some argue that such regulations would hurt businesses, the long-term health of our planet is more important. Countries that have already banned plastic bags have seen significant improvements in their environment. We must act now to protect our future.'

Analysis: The author presents a clear argument (stricter regulations), supports it with reasons (pollution, harm to marine life), and addresses a counterargument (hurt businesses). The language is persuasive, urging action.
How to Approach Questions on Persuasive Passages

items: Identify the author's main claim or thesis.
Look for the reasons and evidence given to support the claim.
Recognize persuasive techniques such as emotional appeal, appeal to logic, or use of authority.
Consider whether the author addresses opposing views.

blocks.text: Practice Question Read the passage and answer the question. 'The introduction of a national minimum wage is not only necessary but also long overdue. No worker in this country should be forced to live below the poverty line. A decent wage boosts workers' morale, increases productivity, and reduces the need for government welfare programs. Opponents argue that it will lead to job losses, but studies have shown that the benefits far outweigh the costs.' What is the author's main argument? A. Workers are not productive enough. B. A national minimum wage should be introduced. C. Government welfare programs are ineffective. D. Job losses are inevitable with a minimum wage.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The author clearly states that the minimum wage is necessary and overdue, and provides reasons to support this view. The other options are either supporting details or opposing views.

lessons.title: Words in Context
lessons.summary: Understanding the meaning of individual words as they are used in a passage, focusing on nuance and connotation.

blocks.text: While 'Vocabulary in Context' (1.5) focuses on determining the meaning of unfamiliar words, 'Words in Context' goes further by examining the nuance, connotation, and specific meaning of a word as it fits into the overall tone and meaning of the passage. JAMB may ask you to identify the most appropriate synonym or explain why a particular word is used.
Key Concepts

items: Denotation: The literal dictionary definition of a word.
Connotation: The emotional or cultural associations a word carries (e.g., 'home' vs. 'house').
Contextual Meaning: How the word is used in the specific sentence or paragraph.

blocks.title: Word Choice and Connotation
blocks.text:
Sentence: 'The politician was persistent in his pursuit of the bill.' vs. 'The politician was stubborn in his pursuit of the bill.'

Analysis: Both words indicate not giving up, but 'persistent' has a positive connotation (determined, hardworking), while 'stubborn' has a negative connotation (obstinate, unreasonable). The author's choice reveals their attitude.

Practice Question In the passage below, which word best captures the author's intended meaning for 'ambitious'? 'Her ambitious plan to start a charity was met with skepticism, but she pressed on, determined to make a difference.' A. Overconfident B. Determined C. Greedy D. Unrealistic

Correct Answer: B Explanation: In this context, 'ambitious' means having a strong desire to achieve something, which is synonymous with 'determined'. The other options carry negative or different connotations.

lessons.title: Phrases in Context
lessons.summary: Understanding the meaning and function of phrases within a passage.

blocks.text: A phrase is a group of words that works together as a unit but does not contain a subject and a verb. In comprehension, you may need to interpret the meaning of a phrase, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, or prepositional phrase, within the context of the passage. The meaning of a phrase often depends on its surrounding words.
Common Types of Phrases

items: Noun Phrase: Functions as a noun (e.g., 'the old man in the corner').
Verb Phrase: Functions as a verb (e.g., 'has been running').
Prepositional Phrase: Begins with a preposition and functions as an adjective or adverb (e.g., 'under the table').
Participial Phrase: Begins with a participle and acts as an adjective (e.g., 'running quickly, she...').

blocks.title: Interpreting a Phrase
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The politician, in a moment of rare candour, admitted his mistake.'

Question: What does the phrase 'in a moment of rare candour' mean?

Answer: It means that the politician was being unusually honest and open at that moment.

Practice Question In the sentence, 'The students, having finished their exams, celebrated wildly,' what does the phrase 'having finished their exams' describe? A. The reason for celebration. B. The time of celebration. C. The students themselves. D. The exams themselves.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The participial phrase 'having finished their exams' modifies the noun 'students,' describing which students—those who have completed exams.

lessons.title: Clauses in Context
lessons.summary: Understanding the role of clauses in a sentence and how they contribute to meaning.

blocks.text: A clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb. There are independent clauses (complete sentences) and dependent clauses (cannot stand alone). In comprehension, understanding clause structure can help you interpret complex sentences, identify relationships between ideas, and answer questions about sentence function.
Types of Clauses

items: Independent Clause: Can stand alone as a sentence. (e.g., 'The sun set.')
Dependent Clause: Cannot stand alone; often begins with subordinating conjunctions like 'because,' 'although,' 'when.' (e.g., 'Although the sun set...')
Relative Clause: A dependent clause that modifies a noun, introduced by 'who,' 'which,' 'that.' (e.g., 'The man who came to dinner...')

blocks.title: Analyzing Clauses
blocks.text:
Sentence: 'Although he was tired, he finished the project.'

  • Dependent clause: 'Although he was tired' (cannot stand alone).
  • Independent clause: 'he finished the project' (can stand alone).

The dependent clause provides context (concession) for the main action.

Practice Question In the sentence 'The book that I borrowed from the library is due tomorrow,' what is the function of the clause 'that I borrowed from the library'? A. It is the main clause. B. It modifies the verb. C. It modifies the noun 'book'. D. It expresses a condition.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The clause 'that I borrowed from the library' is a relative clause that gives more information about the noun 'book'.

lessons.title: Sentences in Context
lessons.summary: Understanding the meaning and function of different sentence types within a passage.

blocks.text: A sentence is a grammatical unit that expresses a complete thought. In comprehension, the type and structure of a sentence can affect its meaning and emphasis. JAMB may ask you to interpret the meaning of a sentence, identify its purpose (statement, question, command, exclamation), or understand how it contributes to the passage's overall meaning.
Sentence Types by Function

items: Declarative: Makes a statement. (e.g., 'The sky is blue.')
Interrogative: Asks a question. (e.g., 'Is the sky blue?')
Imperative: Gives a command or request. (e.g., 'Look at the sky.')
Exclamatory: Expresses strong emotion. (e.g., 'What a beautiful sky!')

blocks.title: Sentence Type and Meaning
blocks.text:
Sentence: 'Can you believe the price of fuel?'

This is an interrogative sentence, but in context it might be used as a rhetorical question to express disbelief, not to seek information.
Practice Question What is the main purpose of the sentence 'Please submit your assignments by Friday'? A. To make a statement. B. To ask a question. C. To give a command. D. To express excitement.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The sentence is a polite command (imperative) instructing the reader to submit assignments by a deadline.

lessons.title: Figures of Speech
lessons.summary: Identifying and interpreting common figures of speech such as simile, metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.

blocks.text: A figure of speech is a word or phrase that is used in a non-literal way to create a rhetorical effect. They are common in literature and persuasive writing. In comprehension, you may be asked to identify a figure of speech and explain its effect on meaning. Common figures tested include simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, and irony.
Common Figures of Speech

blocks.caption: Figures of Speech with Examples
rows: A direct comparison not using 'like' or 'as'.
Giving human qualities to inanimate objects.
Saying the opposite of what is meant.

blocks.title: Interpreting Figures of Speech
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The sun smiled down on the children playing in the park.'

Figure: Personification (the sun is given the human action of smiling).

Effect: It creates a warm, pleasant atmosphere.
Practice Question What figure of speech is used in the sentence 'The news hit him like a ton of bricks'? A. Metaphor B. Simile C. Personification D. Hyperbole
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The comparison uses 'like' to compare the impact of the news to a heavy weight, which is a simile.

lessons.title: Idioms in Comprehension
lessons.summary: Understanding and interpreting idiomatic expressions within a passage.

blocks.text: Idioms are expressions whose meaning is not predictable from the literal meanings of the individual words. In comprehension passages, idioms are often used to convey a point in a vivid or concise way. You may be asked to explain the meaning of an idiom as it is used in the passage.
Strategies for Idioms

items: Consider the context—what is the overall message of the sentence or paragraph?
Think about the figurative meaning—what is the speaker implying?
Eliminate literal interpretations that do not fit.

blocks.title: Interpreting an Idiom
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The manager was at his wits' end trying to resolve the dispute.'

Meaning: The manager was very frustrated and did not know what to do next.

Practice Question What is the meaning of the underlined idiom in the sentence? 'When it came to negotiating, the young lawyer cut his teeth on a high-profile case.' A. Gained his first experience. B. Lost his teeth. C. Made a lot of money. D. Won the case easily.
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Cut his teeth' means to gain initial experience in a particular field.

lessons.title: Grammatical Functions
lessons.summary: How grammatical structures (subject, object, complement, etc.) contribute to meaning in comprehension.

blocks.text: Understanding grammatical functions can help you interpret the relationships between parts of a sentence. In comprehension, you may need to identify the subject, object, complement, or modifier to understand the sentence's meaning and the author's emphasis.
Key Grammatical Functions

items: Subject: The doer of the action or the topic of the sentence.
Predicate: The part of the sentence that tells something about the subject.
Object: The receiver of the action (direct object) or the recipient (indirect object).
Complement: A word or phrase that completes the meaning of the subject or object.
Modifier: A word or phrase that describes another element.

blocks.title: Analyzing Grammatical Function
blocks.text:
Sentence: 'The committee gave the award to the student.'

  • Subject: The committee
  • Verb: gave
  • Direct Object: the award
  • Indirect Object: the student

Understanding these functions clarifies who did what to whom.
Practice Question In the sentence 'The president appointed her as the new minister,' what is the function of 'her'? A. Subject B. Direct Object C. Indirect Object D. Object Complement
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Her' is the receiver of the action 'appointed,' so it is the direct object.

lessons.title: Writer's Intention
lessons.summary: Identifying why the writer wrote the passage, going beyond purpose to specific aims.

blocks.text: While purpose (1.6) is general, intention is more specific: what did the writer hope to achieve with this particular passage? For example, the purpose might be to persuade, but the intention could be to evoke sympathy, to motivate action, or to criticize. Questions on intention require you to consider the writer's tone, word choice, and the passage's overall effect.
How to Determine Writer's Intention

items: Look at the author's attitude (tone) towards the subject.
Consider the effects of specific words and phrases.
Ask: 'What does the author want the reader to think or feel after reading this?'

blocks.title: Intention Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The government's new policy, while well-intentioned, is doomed to fail because it ignores the root causes of poverty.'

Intention: The writer intends to criticize the policy and suggest that it is ineffective, while acknowledging its good intentions.

Practice Question What is the writer's intention in the following passage? 'The current educational system is a relic of the colonial era, designed to produce clerks, not critical thinkers. It is time for a radical overhaul that prioritizes creativity and problem-solving.' A. To inform about the history of education. B. To argue for a change in the educational system. C. To criticize colonial rule. D. To explain the importance of critical thinking.
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The writer is not just criticizing; the phrase 'it is time for a radical overhaul' clearly expresses the intention to persuade readers that change is needed.

lessons.title: Writer's Opinion
lessons.summary: Distinguishing the writer's personal views from factual information in a passage.

blocks.text: In many passages, the author presents both facts and opinions. Being able to distinguish between them is a key skill. Facts are verifiable; opinions are subjective judgments. In JAMB, you may be asked to identify the author's opinion on a particular issue or to separate fact from opinion.
Identifying Fact vs. Opinion

items: Facts: Statements that can be proven true or false. Often include statistics, dates, or objective descriptions.
Opinions: Beliefs, judgments, or personal feelings. Often signaled by words like 'think,' 'believe,' 'should,' 'best,' 'worst.'

blocks.title: Fact vs. Opinion Example
blocks.text:
• Fact: 'Nigeria became independent in 1960.'
  • Opinion: 'Nigeria is the best country in Africa.'

Practice Question Which of the following statements from a passage is an opinion? A. 'The GDP grew by 2.5% last year.' B. 'The government should invest more in education.' C. 'The unemployment rate is 15%.' D. 'The capital city is Abuja.'
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Should' indicates a recommendation, which is a subjective opinion. The others are objective facts.

lessons.title: Coherence and Logical Reasoning
lessons.summary: Understanding how ideas are organized and connected in a passage to form a logical whole.

blocks.text: Coherence refers to the logical flow of ideas in a passage. A coherent passage presents ideas in a clear, orderly manner, with transitions that show relationships between sentences and paragraphs. Logical reasoning questions may ask you to identify the pattern of organization (e.g., cause-effect, compare-contrast) or to determine which sentence best fits in a paragraph.
Common Organizational Patterns

items: Chronological: Events in time order.
Cause and Effect: One event leads to another.
Compare and Contrast: Showing similarities and differences.
Problem and Solution: Presenting a problem and then offering a solution.
Classification: Grouping items into categories.

blocks.title: Identifying Organization
blocks.text:
Passage: 'First, we must acknowledge the scale of the problem. Second, we need to identify the root causes. Third, we can propose solutions.'

Pattern: Chronological/sequential.

Practice Question What is the organizational pattern of the following passage? 'Unlike traditional schools, online learning offers flexibility. However, it also requires self-discipline. While both methods have their strengths, the choice depends on individual learning styles.' A. Compare and contrast B. Cause and effect C. Problem and solution D. Chronological
Correct Answer: A Explanation: The passage compares traditional schools and online learning, highlighting differences and similarities.

lessons.title: Cloze Test
lessons.summary: Strategies for answering cloze test (fill-in-the-blank) questions in comprehension passages.

blocks.text: A cloze test is a passage with certain words removed. You are required to fill in the blanks with the most appropriate word from given options. This tests your understanding of vocabulary, grammar, and overall coherence. Cloze tests are common in JAMB comprehension.
Strategies for Cloze Tests

items: Read the entire passage first to get the general idea.
For each blank, consider the grammatical context (e.g., part of speech, tense, agreement).
Look for clues in the surrounding sentences—they often provide synonyms, contrasts, or explanations.
Choose the option that best fits the meaning and grammar of the whole passage.
Eliminate options that are clearly wrong.

blocks.title: Cloze Test Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'The new policy was designed to ___ economic growth, but it has been ___ by critics.'

Options for first blank: A. hinder, B. stimulate, C. ignore, D. prevent.

Options for second blank: A. praised, B. criticized, C. implemented, D. ignored.

Answer: The first blank should be 'stimulate' (to encourage growth), and the second should be 'criticized' (since critics disagree). The correct choices are B and B.
Practice Question Choose the best option to fill the blank. 'The athlete's dedication to training was , and it ultimately led to her success.' A. inconsistent B. rewarding C. unwavering D. tiresome
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The sentence says dedication led to success, so the dedication must have been constant and strong. 'Unwavering' fits best.

lessons.title: Synthesis of Ideas
lessons.summary: Combining information from different parts of a passage to draw conclusions or form a new idea.

blocks.text: Synthesis is the process of combining separate pieces of information to create a new whole. In comprehension, you may need to synthesize ideas from different paragraphs to answer a question that requires seeing the big picture. This is a higher-order skill often tested in JAMB.
How to Synthesize Ideas

items: Identify the main points in each part of the passage.
Look for connections or relationships between these points.
Combine them to answer a question that covers the entire passage or a large portion.

blocks.title: Synthesis Example
blocks.text:
Passage: (Paragraph 1) 'Nigeria has a young population with great potential.' (Paragraph 2) 'However, high unemployment rates hinder economic growth.' (Paragraph 3) 'Investment in education and vocational training can address this.'

Synthesis: Nigeria's young population offers potential, but unemployment is a challenge; investing in education can help overcome it.

Practice Question Read the following statements from a passage and synthesize the overall message. 'Statement 1: Climate change is causing more extreme weather events.' 'Statement 2: Agriculture is highly dependent on weather patterns.' 'Statement 3: Food security is at risk in many parts of the world.' A. Climate change has no impact on agriculture. B. Extreme weather events are the only cause of food insecurity. C. Climate change threatens food security through its effects on agriculture. D. Agriculture is not affected by weather.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: Combining the three statements leads to the logical conclusion that climate change (extreme weather) affects agriculture, which in turn threatens food security.

lessons.title: Summary Techniques
lessons.summary: How to effectively summarize a passage by identifying key points and condensing them.

blocks.text: A summary is a concise restatement of the main ideas of a passage in your own words. JAMB may ask you to summarize a passage or part of it. Good summary skills require you to distinguish between essential and non-essential information, and to express ideas clearly and concisely.
Steps to Write a Summary

items: Read the passage carefully to understand the main ideas.
Identify the thesis and the key supporting points.
Eliminate examples, repetitions, and minor details.
Rewrite the main ideas in your own words.
Ensure your summary is concise and coherent.

blocks.title: Summary Example
blocks.text:
Passage: 'Social media has transformed communication. It allows instant connection across the globe, but it also has downsides such as misinformation and reduced face-to-face interaction. Despite the challenges, social media remains a powerful tool for spreading information and mobilizing communities.'

Summary: Social media revolutionizes communication globally, but poses risks like misinformation and less personal interaction; nonetheless, it is a powerful tool for information and community action.

Practice Question Which of the following is the best summary of the passage below? 'The importance of regular exercise cannot be overstated. It improves cardiovascular health, boosts mood, and helps with weight management. Many people avoid exercise due to lack of time, but even short daily sessions can make a difference.' A. Exercise is important for health and can be done even in short amounts. B. People are too busy to exercise. C. Exercise only helps with weight management. D. Regular exercise is the only way to be healthy.
Correct Answer: A Explanation: Option A captures the two main points: the importance of exercise and the feasibility of short sessions. Options B, C, and D are incomplete or misrepresent the passage.

lessons.title: Comprehension Question Types
lessons.summary: An overview of the different types of comprehension questions and how to approach each.

blocks.text: JAMB comprehension questions can be classified into several types based on what they ask. Understanding these types can help you anticipate what to look for when reading the passage. Common types include: main idea, detail, inference, vocabulary, tone, purpose, and summary questions.

blocks.caption: Question Types and Strategies
rows: Look for the topic sentence or overall summary.
Scan the passage for key terms.
Read between the lines; combine clues.
What does this word mean here?
Analyze word choice and emotional language.
Why did the author write this?
Ask: Is it to inform, persuade, entertain, or explain?
Provide a concise restatement of the passage.

blocks.text: Practice Question Which question type asks you to find the author's attitude towards the subject? A. Main Idea B. Supporting Detail C. Tone D. Purpose
Correct Answer: C Explanation: Tone questions specifically ask about the author's attitude, which is conveyed through word choice and style.

lessons.title: Full JAMB Comprehension Practice
lessons.summary: A full-length practice passage with questions to test all comprehension skills.

blocks.text: Now it's time to put all the skills you've learned together. Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow. This exercise will test your ability to identify the main idea, understand supporting details, make inferences, understand vocabulary in context, and identify tone and purpose.
Passage

The rapid urbanization of Nigeria has presented both unprecedented opportunities and significant challenges. In recent decades, rural-to-urban migration has accelerated, driven primarily by the search for economic prospects. Cities like Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt have swelled, becoming bustling hubs of commerce and innovation. This influx has provided a crucial labor force for the growing industrial and service sectors, contributing substantially to the nation's GDP. However, the strain on urban infrastructure has been immense. Housing shortages, overwhelmed transportation systems, inadequate water and sanitation facilities, and mounting waste management problems have become endemic features of many Nigerian cities. Furthermore, the rising cost of living and the competitive labor market often leave the poorest migrants trapped in sprawling, underserved slums, where unemployment and crime are rife. Addressing the complex issues of urbanization, therefore, requires a multifaceted approach that combines effective urban planning, substantial investment in infrastructure, and inclusive economic policies that ensure the benefits of city life are shared by all.
Questions

1. What is the main idea of the passage? A. Lagos is the most urbanized city in Nigeria. B. Urbanization in Nigeria brings both good and bad consequences. C. The government is not doing enough to manage urbanization. D. Rural-to-urban migration is driven by the search for jobs.
2. According to the passage, which of the following is a benefit of urbanization? A. Improved housing for all. B. A reliable water supply. C. Economic growth and innovation. D. Reduced crime rates.
3. The word 'endemic' as used in the passage most likely means... A. Rare and unusual. B. Limited to a specific area. C. Constantly and frequently found. D. Newly introduced.

4. It can be inferred from the passage that the author believes... A. Urbanization is a problem with no solution. B. The challenges of urbanization can be solved. C. Rural life is superior to urban life. D. Slums are the only option for poor migrants.
5. The tone of the passage can best be described as... A. Pessimistic and despairing. B. Sarcastic and mocking. C. Objective and balanced. D. Celebratory and joyful.
Answers and Explanations

1. Correct Answer: B Explanation: The passage clearly presents both the opportunities (economic prospects, labor force, GDP) and the challenges (housing shortages, infrastructure strain, slums) of urbanization. Options A and D are specific details, and option C is an inference that is not directly supported by the text.

2. Correct Answer: C Explanation: The passage states that cities have 'become bustling hubs of commerce and innovation' and that the influx of people has 'contributed substantially to the nation's GDP.' This supports economic growth and innovation. The other options are presented as challenges or are not mentioned.

3. Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Endemic' is used to describe the problems of housing shortages, poor transport, etc. The phrase 'become endemic features' suggests these problems are widespread and persistent in many cities. 'Constantly and frequently found' is the best match.

4. Correct Answer: B Explanation: The author states that addressing the issues 'requires a multifaceted approach...' This implies that the author believes there are solutions. Therefore, the challenges are not unsolvable. Option A is incorrect because a solution is proposed. Options C and D are not supported by the text.

5. Correct Answer: C Explanation: The author presents both sides of the issue, the positive and the negative, without using heavily emotional or opinionated language. The purpose seems to be to provide an overview of the topic. Therefore, the tone is objective and balanced.

lessons.title: Comprehension Revision
lessons.summary: A concise summary of the key comprehension skills and strategies for JAMB.

blocks.text: Key Comprehension Skills Summary

blocks.caption: Skill Recap
rows: The central point of the passage.
Ask: 'What is the author's one big point?' Look for topic sentences.
Facts, examples, and evidence supporting the main idea.
Scan for specific information. Watch out for distorting traps.
A logical conclusion based on evidence, not explicitly stated.
'Read between the lines.' Ask: 'What is implied?' Ensure you have textual support.
The meaning of a word as used in the passage.
Use context clues: definition, synonym, antonym, inference.
The author's attitude and reason for writing.
Analyze word choice (tone). Ask: 'Is the author informing, persuading, or entertaining?'

blocks.text: Examination Reminders

items: Always read the passage carefully, maybe even twice, before looking at the questions.
For main idea questions, eliminate options that are too broad or too narrow.
For detail questions, locate the specific part of the passage and read carefully. Watch for the 'one-word' trap.
For inference questions, never choose an answer that is directly stated. The correct answer is always implied.
For vocabulary questions, always let the context, not your dictionary knowledge, be your guide.
To identify tone, focus on the author's choice of words (adjectives, verbs).
Manage your time effectively. Don't spend too long on one question.

blocks.text: The more you practice, the better you will become. Regular practice with a wide variety of passages is the best way to master these skills.

lessons.title: Introduction to Lexis and Structure
lessons.summary: An overview of the 'Lexis and Structure' section, covering vocabulary, grammar, and correct English usage.

blocks.text: The 'Lexis and Structure' section of JAMB Use of English is a comprehensive test of your knowledge of English vocabulary and grammar. It covers a wide range of topics, from choosing the right word to understanding complex sentence structures. A strong grasp of this section is essential for scoring high marks, as it forms the backbone of the entire paper.
What is 'Lexis'?

Lexis refers to the vocabulary of a language. In this context, it means your knowledge of words. This includes not just their dictionary definitions, but also their synonyms, antonyms, and how they are used in different contexts. The JAMB vocabulary section tests your ability to distinguish between similar words, understand idiomatic expressions, and use words appropriately.
The total stock of words in a language; the vocabulary.
What is 'Structure'?

Structure refers to the rules of grammar that govern how words are arranged to form meaningful sentences. This is often what people mean when they talk about 'correct English.' It includes parts of speech, tenses, subject-verb agreement, question tags, reported speech, and many other grammatical rules. JAMB tests your ability to identify and apply these rules correctly.
The grammatical rules and principles governing the arrangement of words into sentences.
Why is 'Lexis and Structure' Important for JAMB?

items: A large number of questions are directly from this section, including sentence completion, error identification, and fill-in-the-blank questions.
Your performance in this section shows the examiners your command of the English language.
It forms the foundation for other parts of the exam, like comprehension and continuous writing. You need strong grammar to write a good essay and understand complex passages.

blocks.text: The best way to prepare for the Lexis and Structure section is to combine consistent study of grammatical rules with extensive reading. Reading widely exposes you to correct sentence structures and a variety of vocabulary in context.

lessons.title: Parts of Speech
lessons.summary: A comprehensive review of the eight parts of speech and their functions in English sentences.

blocks.text: Every word in an English sentence belongs to a category known as a part of speech. Understanding these categories is fundamental to understanding grammar. A word's part of speech tells us what job it does in a sentence. There are eight traditional parts of speech in English.
The Eight Parts of Speech

items: Noun: A person, place, thing, or idea. (e.g., Olu, Lagos, book, happiness)
Pronoun: Replaces a noun. (e.g., he, she, it, they, we)
Verb: An action, occurrence, or state of being. (e.g., run, eat, sleep, is, become)
Adjective: Modifies a noun or pronoun. (e.g., beautiful, tall, red, intelligent)
Adverb: Modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. (e.g., quickly, very, quite, well)
Preposition: Shows the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and another word in the sentence. (e.g., in, on, at, to, from, under)
Conjunction: Joins words, phrases, or clauses. (e.g., and, but, or, because, although)
Interjection: An exclamation expressing emotion. (e.g., Wow! Ouch! Hello!)

blocks.caption: Parts of Speech with Examples in Sentences
rows: Describes a verb, adj., or adv.

blocks.text: Many words can function as different parts of speech depending on how they are used in a sentence. For example, 'light' can be a noun ('The light is bright.'), an adjective ('She wore a light dress.'), and a verb ('Please light the candle.'). The word's function in the sentence determines its part of speech.

blocks.title: Identifying Parts of Speech
blocks.text:
Sentence: The young boy quickly ran into the house.

  • young = Adjective (modifies the noun 'boy')
  • boy = Noun (the subject of the sentence)
  • quickly = Adverb (modifies the verb 'ran')
  • ran = Verb (the action)
  • into = Preposition (shows the relationship between 'ran' and 'house')
  • house = Noun (the object of the preposition)
Practice Question 1 Identify the part of speech of the underlined word in the following sentence. 'The beautiful painting was sold at a high price.' A. Adverb B. Noun C. Verb D. Adjective
Correct Answer: D Explanation: The word 'beautiful' describes the noun 'painting.' Words that describe nouns are adjectives.
Practice Question 2 Identify the part of speech of the underlined word in the following sentence. 'The boy is extremely clever.' A. Adjective B. Adverb C. Verb D. Preposition
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Extremely' modifies the adjective 'clever.' Words that modify adjectives are adverbs.
Practice Question 3 Identify the part of speech of the underlined word in the following sentence. 'He and I are going to the market.' A. Preposition B. Conjunction C. Interjection D. Pronoun
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'And' is used to join two words or ideas ('He' and 'I'). This is the function of a conjunction.

lessons.title: Nouns
lessons.summary: A detailed look at nouns, including their types (proper, common, collective, abstract, concrete) and their functions.

blocks.text: A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing, or idea. It is one of the most fundamental parts of speech. Understanding the different types of nouns is important for mastering concepts like subject-verb agreement and pronoun agreement.
Types of Nouns

items: Proper Nouns: Name specific people, places, or things. They are always capitalized. (e.g., Ade, Lagos, Nigeria, December)
Common Nouns: Name general items or ideas. They are not capitalized unless they start a sentence. (e.g., city, boy, country, month)
Concrete Nouns: Things you can see, touch, hear, smell, or taste. (e.g., table, tree, water, music)
Abstract Nouns: Ideas, feelings, or qualities that you cannot perceive with your senses. (e.g., love, courage, intelligence, freedom)
Collective Nouns: Words that refer to a group of people or things as a single unit. (e.g., team, family, audience, flock, swarm)
Countable Nouns: Things you can count. (e.g., one book, two pens, three apples)
Uncountable Nouns: Things you cannot count. (e.g., water, rice, sand, information, money)

blocks.caption: Noun Types at a Glance
rows: Can be perceived by the senses

blocks.text: A word that functions as the name of a specific object or set of objects, such as living creatures, places, actions, qualities, states of existence, or ideas.

blocks.title: Examples of Nouns
blocks.text:
• Person: Aisha, doctor, mother, Daniel
  • Place: Abuja, market, school, beach
  • Thing: table, phone, tree, car
  • Idea: democracy, happiness, knowledge, friendship
A word like 'team' is a singular noun (one team) even though it refers to a group of people. This is important for subject-verb agreement: 'The team is playing well' (singular verb).
Practice Question 1 Identify the type of noun of the underlined word. 'The jury has reached its verdict.' A. Proper B. Abstract C. Collective D. Concrete
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Jury' refers to a group of people, making it a collective noun.
Practice Question 2 Identify the type of noun of the underlined word. 'She was filled with a sense of pride.' A. Abstract B. Concrete C. Proper D. Collective
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Pride' is a feeling or quality, an idea that cannot be physically touched. This is an abstract noun.

lessons.title: Pronouns
lessons.summary: A comprehensive guide to pronouns, including their types, case, and agreement with antecedents.

blocks.text: A pronoun is a word that is used in place of a noun (or another pronoun). The noun that a pronoun refers to is called its antecedent. Pronouns are essential for avoiding repetitive and clumsy sentences. Mastering pronoun usage, especially their case and agreement, is vital for JAMB.
Common Types of Pronouns

items: Personal Pronouns: Refer to specific people or things. (e.g., I, you, he, she, it, we, they; and their object forms: me, him, her, us, them).
Possessive Pronouns: Indicate possession. (e.g., mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs).
Reflexive Pronouns: Refer back to the subject of the sentence. (e.g., myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves).
Demonstrative Pronouns: Point to specific things. (e.g., this, that, these, those).
Indefinite Pronouns: Refer to non-specific people or things. (e.g., everyone, someone, nobody, each, all, both, few, many).
Relative Pronouns: Introduce a relative clause. (e.g., who, whom, which, that, whose).
Interrogative Pronouns: Used to ask questions. (e.g., who, whom, which, what).

blocks.text: Pronoun Case
Pronoun case refers to the form a pronoun takes based on its function in a sentence. There are three main cases.

blocks.caption: Pronoun Case
rows: Acts as the subject of the verb.
I, you, he, she, it, we, they, who
Acts as the object of the verb or preposition.
me, you, him, her, it, us, them, whom
my/mine, your/yours, his, her/hers, its, our/ours, their/theirs, whose

blocks.title: Examples of Pronoun Case
blocks.text:
• Subjective: 'She went to the market.' ('She' is the subject)
  • Objective: 'I gave it to him.' ('him' is the object of the preposition 'to')
  • Possessive: 'That book is mine.' ('mine' shows ownership)
Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement
A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number (singular/plural) and gender (masculine/feminine/neuter).

blocks.title: Agreement
blocks.text:
• Correct: 'The student submitted his assignment.' (Singular 'student' → singular pronoun 'his')
  • Incorrect: 'The student submitted their assignment.' (Singular 'student' → plural pronoun 'their')

A common JAMB trap involves indefinite pronouns. For example, 'Everyone' is singular and requires a singular pronoun. Correct: 'Everyone must bring his or her own pen.' Avoid: 'Everyone must bring their own pen.' (In formal writing, this is often still considered incorrect in JAMB).
Practice Question 1 Select the correct pronoun to complete the sentence. 'Each of the girls must submit assignment by Friday.' A. their B. her C. its D. his or her

Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Each' is a singular indefinite pronoun. Since it refers to 'girls,' the singular feminine pronoun 'her' is the most appropriate choice. While 'his or her' is grammatically correct, 'her' is more elegant and specific.
Practice Question 2 Select the correct pronoun to complete the sentence. 'The award was given to the captain and .' A. I B. me C. myself D. mine
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The pronoun is the object of the preposition 'to.' The objective case is needed, which is 'me.'

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.summary: An in-depth look at verbs, including action verbs, linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, and main verbs.

blocks.text: A verb is a word that describes an action, occurrence, or state of being. It is the heart of a sentence because it tells us what the subject is doing or what is happening to the subject. A sentence is not complete without a verb. Understanding the different types of verbs is crucial for forming correct and meaningful sentences.
Main Types of Verbs

items: Action Verbs: Express a physical or mental action. (e.g., run, play, think, decide, write). Example: 'The boy ran home.'

Linking Verbs: Connect the subject to a word that renames or describes it (subject complement). They do not express action. The most common linking verb is 'to be' (is, am, are, was, were, be, being, been). Other linking verbs include seem, become, appear, feel, smell, taste. Example: 'She is a doctor.'

blocks.text: Auxiliary Verbs (Helping Verbs)
An auxiliary verb (or helping verb) is used with a main verb to form a verb phrase, indicating tense, mood, or voice. They cannot stand alone.

items: Primary Auxiliaries: be, do, have. (e.g., 'He is running.', 'They have arrived.', 'I did go.')
Modal Auxiliaries: can, could, will, would, shall, should, may, might, must. They express necessity, possibility, permission, etc. (e.g., 'You must see a doctor.', 'She can sing well.')

blocks.caption: Action vs. Linking Verbs
rows: 'The dog bit the postman.' (Physical action) 'I believe you.' (Mental action)
Connects the subject to a description.
'The soup tastes delicious.' (Connects soup to delicious) 'He is a lawyer.' (Connects he to lawyer)

blocks.text: A group of words that includes a main verb and one or more auxiliary verbs. (e.g., has been working, will be finished)

blocks.title: Identifying Verbs
blocks.text:
Sentence: The students have been waiting for the bus for two hours.

  • Verb Phrase: have been waiting
  • Main Verb: waiting
  • Auxiliary Verbs: have been

To test if a verb is a linking verb, try replacing it with a form of 'to be' (is, am, are). If the sentence still makes sense, it is probably a linking verb. Test: 'He looked sad.' → 'He was sad.' (The sentence still makes sense, so 'looked' is a linking verb here.)
Practice Question 1 Which of the following words is a verb in the sentence below? 'The beautiful flowers grew quickly in the garden.' A. beautiful B. grew C. quickly D. garden
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Grew' is the action word in the sentence. 'Beautiful' is an adjective, 'quickly' is an adverb, and 'garden' is a noun.
Practice Question 2 Identify the auxiliary verb in the sentence below. 'The children were playing in the park.' A. children B. playing C. were D. in
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Were' is the auxiliary (helping) verb. It helps the main verb 'playing' to form the past continuous tense.

lessons.title: Tenses
lessons.summary: A comprehensive guide to English tenses, including present, past, and future, and their progressive and perfect forms.

blocks.text: Tenses are verb forms that indicate the time of an action or state of being. English has three main times (present, past, and future) and four aspects (simple, continuous/progressive, perfect, and perfect continuous). This gives us a range of twelve tenses to express precise meanings about when and how an action occurs. Correct usage of tenses is vital for JAMB.
The Three Main Times

items: Present Tense: Actions happening now, general truths, or habits. (e.g., He eats.)
Past Tense: Actions that have already happened. (e.g., He ate.)
Future Tense: Actions that will happen. (e.g., He will eat.)

blocks.text: The Four Aspects

blocks.caption: Tense Aspects Explained
rows: A single, completed, or habitual action.
A completed action with a connection to another time.
I have eaten. (just now/completed with current relevance)
An ongoing action that has been happening for a period of time.
I have been eating. (started in the past and is still happening)

blocks.text: Examples of the 12 Tenses (Using 'read')
A set of forms taken by a verb to indicate the time (and sometimes the continuation or completion) of the action or state.
Be careful with irregular verbs. The past tense and past participle forms of irregular verbs can be tricky and are often tested in JAMB. (e.g., sing-sang-sung; swim-swam-swum; write-wrote-written)

blocks.title: Tense Usage Examples
blocks.text:
• Present Simple: 'The sun rises in the east.' (General truth)
  • Present Continuous: 'I am studying for my JAMB.' (Happening now)
  • Past Simple: 'We visited the museum yesterday.' (Completed past action)
  • Present Perfect: 'I have never seen that film.' (Experience up to now)
  • Past Perfect: 'When I arrived, they had already left.' (One past action before another)
  • Future Simple: 'I will call you tomorrow.' (Future intention)
Practice Question 1 Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence. 'By the time he gets home, she dinner.' A. will have cooked B. is cooking C. cooked D. has been cooking
Correct Answer: A Explanation: This sentence describes an action that will be completed before another future action ('he gets home'). This requires the future perfect tense ('will have cooked').
Practice Question 2 Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence. 'I to Lagos many times.' A. have been B. am going C. will go D. went
Correct Answer: A Explanation: The sentence refers to an experience that has happened at some indefinite time in the past. The present perfect tense ('have been') is used for this purpose.

lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement (Basic)
lessons.summary: A detailed explanation of the fundamental rules governing agreement between subjects and verbs in English.

blocks.text: Subject-Verb Agreement (also called Concord) is a fundamental rule of English grammar: a verb must agree with its subject in number (singular or plural). A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. This lesson covers the basic rules. More advanced and exceptional cases are covered in lesson 2.26.
Basic Rule
Singular subject → Singular verb (e.g., He runs.) Plural subject → Plural verb (e.g., They run.)

blocks.title: Basic Agreement
blocks.text:
• Correct: 'The boy plays football.' (Singular: boy → plays)
  • Correct: 'The boys play football.' (Plural: boys → play)
Common Basic Rules

items: Compound subjects joined by 'and' are usually plural.
Subjects joined by 'or/nor' — verb agrees with the nearest subject.
Collective nouns usually take singular verbs when acting as a unit.
Indefinite pronouns like 'each,' 'everyone,' 'nobody' are singular.
Phrases like 'as well as' do not change the number of the subject.

blocks.text: Practice Question Select the correct verb. 'Either the manager or his assistants responsible for the delay.' A. is B. are
Correct Answer: B Explanation: With 'or/nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject, which is 'assistants' (plural), so 'are' is correct.

lessons.title: Question Tags
lessons.summary: A comprehensive guide to the structure, rules, and usage of question tags.

blocks.text: A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement. It is used to confirm information or to ask for agreement. It transforms a statement into a question. The structure of a question tag follows a predictable pattern, but it has some important rules and exceptions that are commonly tested in JAMB.
The Basic Rule
The core rule of question tags is simple: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag.

blocks.title: Basic Tag Formation
blocks.text:
• Positive statement: 'You are coming, aren't you?'
  • Negative statement: 'You aren't coming, are you?'
How to Form a Question Tag

items: Identify the auxiliary verb (helping verb) or a form of 'be' in the statement. This will be the verb in the tag. If there is no auxiliary verb, use do, does, or did.
Identify the subject of the statement and replace it with the correct pronoun in the tag.
Determine the polarity (positive or negative). If the statement is positive, make the tag negative. If the statement is negative, make the tag positive.

blocks.caption: Tag Formation Examples
rows: 'is' is the auxiliary. Positive statement → negative tag.
'can' is the modal. Positive → negative tag.
No auxiliary, use 'did'. Positive → negative tag.
'don't' is in the statement. Negative → positive tag.

blocks.text: Special Cases and Exceptions

items: The verb 'have': When 'have' is a main verb, use 'do', 'does', or 'did'. (e.g., 'You have a car, don't you?') Exception: If 'have' is part of a perfect tense (auxiliary), use 'have' in the tag. (e.g., 'They have arrived, haven't they?')
The verb 'am': The tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?' (e.g., 'I am correct, aren't I?')
Imperatives: For commands or requests, the tag is usually 'will you?' (e.g., 'Close the window, will you?')
