'Let's' (Let us): The tag is 'shall we?' (e.g., 'Let's go to the cinema, shall we?')
Indefinite pronouns: 'Someone', 'everyone', 'nobody' take the pronoun 'they' in the tag. (e.g., 'Everyone is here, aren't they?')
Negative expressions: Words like 'never', 'hardly', 'seldom', 'barely' make the statement negative, so the tag is positive. (e.g., 'She never goes there, does she?')

blocks.text: A short question formed by an auxiliary verb and a pronoun, added to the end of a statement, often used for confirmation or agreement.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Wrong: 'You have seen the movie, have you?' (Using a positive tag for a positive statement) Right: 'You have seen the movie, haven't you?'
  • Wrong: 'Let's go, will we?' Right: 'Let's go, shall we?'
Practice Question 1 Select the correct question tag to complete the sentence. 'The students haven't submitted their assignments, ?' A. haven't they B. have they C. haven't them D. didn't they
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The statement is negative ('haven't'). Therefore, the tag must be positive ('have they'). Also, the pronoun for 'students' is 'they'.
Practice Question 2 Select the correct question tag to complete the sentence. 'I am the best candidate for the job, ?' A. am I B. am I not C. aren't I D. aren't me
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The tag for 'I am' is a special case: the correct form is 'aren't I?'.
Practice Question 3 Select the correct question tag to complete the sentence. 'Let's pray for peace, ?' A. shall we B. will we C. don't we D. aren't we
Correct Answer: A Explanation: For a sentence starting with 'Let's,' the correct tag is always 'shall we?'.

lessons.title: Conditional Sentences
lessons.summary: A detailed lesson on the structure and usage of conditional sentences (if-clauses) in English.

blocks.text: Conditional sentences are sentences that describe a condition and its result. They typically contain an 'if' clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). Understanding the different types of conditional sentences is crucial for expressing relationships between actions and for performing well in the JAMB Use of English exam.
The Four Main Types of Conditionals

blocks.caption: Types of Conditional Sentences
rows: General truths and laws of nature.
'If I had a million naira, I would travel the world.'
'If he had studied, he would have passed the exam.'

blocks.text: Key Points and Variations

items: Punctuation: When the 'if clause' comes first, it is followed by a comma. When the main clause comes first, no comma is needed. (e.g., 'If you study hard, you will pass.' vs. 'You will pass if you study hard.')
Modals: Other modals like can, could, might, should can be used in the main clause to express different meanings. (e.g., 'If you work hard, you might succeed.')
Unless: Means 'if not' and is often used in first conditional sentences. (e.g., 'Unless you leave now, you will miss the bus.' → 'If you don't leave now, you will miss the bus.')

blocks.text: A sentence that expresses a condition and the consequence of that condition, often using the word 'if'.

blocks.title: Conditional Sentences in Context
blocks.text:
• Zero: 'If you boil water to 100°C, it evaporates.' (Scientific fact)
  • First: 'If the government reduces fuel prices, the cost of living will decrease.' (Real possibility)
  • Second: 'If I were you, I would accept the offer.' (Unreal present situation. Note: 'were' is used for all subjects in the 'if' clause for this type.)
  • Third: 'If he had started the business then, he would have been a millionaire by now.' (Hypothetical past situation)

A common JAMB trap is mixing up the tenses. For example, using 'would have' in the 'if' clause instead of the main clause is a common error. Incorrect: 'If I would have known, I would have come.' Correct: 'If I had known, I would have come.'
Practice Question 1 Choose the correct option to complete the sentence. 'If I you, I would not do that.' A. was B. were C. am D. have been
Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a second conditional sentence (unreal present situation). In the 'if' clause, 'were' is used for all subjects, including 'I'.
Practice Question 2 Choose the correct option to complete the sentence. 'If she earlier, she would have caught the bus.' A. has woken B. will wake C. had woken D. wakes
Correct Answer: C Explanation: This is a third conditional sentence (unreal past). The 'if' clause requires the past perfect ('had woken').

lessons.title: Reported Speech
lessons.summary: A comprehensive guide to converting direct speech to reported speech, including changes to pronouns, tenses, and time expressions.

blocks.text: Reported speech (also called indirect speech) is how we report what someone said without using their exact words. Unlike direct speech, which uses quotation marks ('...'), reported speech often uses 'that' to introduce the reported clause. Mastering reported speech is essential, as it is a common area of testing in JAMB.
The Main Changes
When converting from direct to reported speech, three main things usually change: the verb tense, the pronouns, and the time and place expressions.
1. Pronoun Changes
Pronouns must be changed to reflect the perspective of the reporter.

blocks.title: Pronoun Change
blocks.text: Direct: 'I am happy,' said Ali. Reported: Ali said that he was happy.
2. Tense Changes
If the reporting verb (e.g., said, told) is in the past tense, the tense in the direct speech usually 'backs' (moves backward) in time.

blocks.caption: Tense Backshifting in Reported Speech
rows: 'I bought a car.' → He said he had bought a car.
'I have seen her.' → He said he had seen her.
'I must go.' → He said he had to go.

blocks.text: 3. Time and Place Expression Changes

blocks.caption: Changes in Time and Place Expressions
rows: the previous day / the day before
the next day / the following day

blocks.text: A way of reporting what someone has said without using their exact words, involving changes to pronouns, tenses, and time/place references.

blocks.title: Full Transformation
blocks.text:
Direct: 'I will meet you here tomorrow,' Mary said to John.

Reported: Mary told John that she would meet him there the next day.
If the reporting verb is in the present tense (e.g., says), the tense in the reported clause does not change. Example: 'Mary says: 'I am tired.'' → 'Mary says that she is tired.'

Practice Question 1 Select the correct reported speech version of the sentence below. Direct: 'I have finished my homework,' said Tunde. A. Tunde said that I have finished my homework. B. Tunde said that he had finished his homework. C. Tunde said that he has finished his homework. D. Tunde said that I had finished my homework.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'I' changes to 'he' to match the speaker (Tunde). The reporting verb 'said' is in the past, so 'have finished' (present perfect) changes to 'had finished' (past perfect).

Practice Question 2 Select the correct reported speech version of the sentence below. Direct: 'We are going to the cinema tomorrow,' they said. A. They said that we are going to the cinema tomorrow. B. They said that they were going to the cinema the next day. C. They said that they are going to the cinema the next day. D. They said that we were going to the cinema tomorrow.
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The pronoun 'we' changes to 'they'. 'Are going' (present continuous) changes to 'were going' (past continuous). 'Tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'.

lessons.title: Active and Passive Voice
lessons.summary: An explanation of active and passive voice, how to convert between them, and when each is appropriate.

blocks.text: Voice in English grammar refers to the relationship between the verb and the subject of the sentence. There are two voices: active and passive. Understanding the difference and knowing when to use each is an important part of mastering English structure.
Active Voice
In the active voice, the subject of the sentence performs the action of the verb. This is the most common and direct way to write in English.

blocks.title: Active Voice
blocks.text:
• 'The dog (subject) chased the cat (object).'
  • 'The students (subject) wrote the exam (object).'
Passive Voice

In the passive voice, the subject of the sentence receives the action of the verb. The focus is on the action itself or the receiver of the action, not the doer. It is formed using a form of the verb 'to be' + the past participle of the main verb.

blocks.title: Passive Voice
blocks.text:
• 'The cat (subject) was chased by the dog.'
  • 'The exam (subject) was written by the students.'
How to Convert from Active to Passive

items: Identify the subject, verb, and object in the active sentence.
The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
The verb in the passive sentence is a form of 'to be' + the past participle of the main verb. The tense of 'to be' should match the tense of the active verb.
The subject of the active sentence becomes the agent, introduced by the preposition 'by' (optional).

blocks.caption: Active to Passive Conversion
rows: 'Built' (past simple) → 'was built'. The agent 'by them' is often omitted.
The report is being reviewed by the committee.
The package will be delivered by the company.
The car has been fixed by the mechanic.

blocks.text: The form of a verb that indicates whether the subject of a sentence performs the action (active voice) or receives the action (passive voice).

In JAMB, the passive voice is often tested by asking you to identify the correct passive form of a sentence. Watch out for common errors like using the wrong form of 'to be' or the wrong past participle.

Practice Question 1 Select the correct passive voice form of the sentence below. Active: The children are eating the food. A. The food was eaten by the children. B. The food is being eaten by the children. C. The food has been eaten by the children. D. The food was being eaten by the children.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The active sentence is in the present continuous tense ('are eating'). The passive voice must also be in the present continuous: 'is being eaten'. The object 'the food' becomes the subject.

Practice Question 2 Select the correct active voice form of the sentence below. Passive: The letter was written by the secretary. A. The secretary was writing the letter. B. The secretary writes the letter. C. The secretary wrote the letter. D. The secretary has written the letter.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The passive sentence is in the simple past tense ('was written'). The active voice in the simple past is 'wrote'. The agent 'the secretary' becomes the subject.

lessons.title: Prepositions
lessons.summary: A lesson on common prepositions, their usage, and common mistakes in their application.

blocks.text: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence. They are often small words, but they are crucial for conveying precise meaning, especially about time, place, and direction. Prepositions are frequently tested in JAMB, and using the wrong one is a common mistake.
Common Prepositions

blocks.caption: Common Prepositions by Category
rows: in, on, at, under, over, between, behind, beside, among, near, inside
in, on, at, by, during, for, since, until, after, before
to, from, into, out of, through, across, towards, up, down
of, with, for, about, by, like, as, from

blocks.text: Common Preposition Pitfalls and Mistakes

items: In vs. Into: 'In' is for a position inside something. 'Into' is for movement to the inside of something. (e.g., 'He is in the house.' vs. 'He walked into the house.')
On vs. At: For place, 'on' is used for surfaces, 'at' for specific points. (e.g., 'The book is on the floor.' vs. 'Meet me at the bus stop.')
Since vs. For: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time. 'For' is used with a period of time. (e.g., 'I have been here since 8 AM.' vs. 'I have been here for two hours.')
Different from: The correct phrase is usually 'different from' (not 'to' or 'than'). (e.g., 'My approach is different from yours.')
Angry with: 'Angry with' is used for people. 'Angry about' is used for situations or things. (e.g., 'I am angry with him.' vs. 'I am angry about the result.')

blocks.text: A word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence, often indicating location, direction, or time.

blocks.title: Prepositions in Context
blocks.text:
• In: 'He lives in Abuja.' (Place)
  • At: 'The meeting is at 2 PM.' (Time)
  • By: 'I will finish this by Friday.' (Deadline)
  • For: 'This gift is for you.' (Purpose)
Practice Question 1 Select the correct preposition to complete the sentence. 'She has been waiting for you 3 hours.' A. since B. from C. for D. about
Correct Answer: C Explanation: '3 hours' is a period of time. The preposition 'for' is used with periods of time.
Practice Question 2 Select the correct preposition to complete the sentence. 'The teacher was angry the students for making noise.' A. about B. with C. on D. from
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Angry with' is the correct preposition to use when referring to people.

lessons.title: Conjunctions
lessons.summary: A lesson on conjunctions, their types (coordinating, subordinating, correlative), and their use in sentences.

blocks.text: A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases, or clauses together. They are the 'connectors' of the English language, and they are essential for creating complex and coherent sentences. Conjunctions are frequently tested in JAMB through sentence completion and error identification.
The Three Main Types of Conjunctions

items: Coordinating Conjunctions: These join words, phrases, or independent clauses that are grammatically equal. Remember them with the acronym FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. (e.g., 'I like tea, but she likes coffee.')

Subordinating Conjunctions: These join an independent clause with a dependent clause. They show a relationship like time, cause, condition, or contrast. (e.g., because, although, since, when, while, unless, if, until, after, before). (e.g., 'I went home because I was tired.')

Correlative Conjunctions: These are pairs of conjunctions that work together to join equal elements. (e.g., either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or). (e.g., 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present.')

blocks.caption: Types of Conjunctions with Examples
rows: 'I wanted to go out, <u>but</u> it was raining.'
'He passed the exam <u>because</u> he studied hard.'

blocks.text: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses.

blocks.title: Using Conjunctions Correctly
blocks.text:
• Coordinating: 'She is kind and generous.' (joining words)
  • Subordinating: 'Although he was tired, he finished the race.' (showing contrast)
  • Correlative: 'The hotel was both comfortable and affordable.' (pairing adjectives)

A common JAMB trap involves 'neither...nor' and 'either...or'. The verb must agree with the subject closer to it. Correct: 'Neither the man nor his children are at home.' Incorrect: 'Neither the man nor his children is at home.'
Practice Question 1 Select the correct conjunction to complete the sentence. 'He was hungry, he ate a large meal.' A. but B. so C. although D. because
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The first clause is a cause, and the second is a result. 'So' correctly shows this cause-and-effect relationship. 'Because' would reverse the logic.
Practice Question 2 Select the correct conjunction to complete the sentence. ' the rain, the match continued.' A. Because of B. Despite C. Although D. Since

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The sentence shows a contrast. 'Despite' is a preposition that can be followed by a noun ('the rain'). 'Although' is a conjunction and needs a clause: 'Although it rained...'

lessons.title: Phrasal Verbs
lessons.summary: An introduction to phrasal verbs, their meanings, and how they are used in English.

blocks.text: A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a preposition or an adverb (or both). The combination creates a meaning that is often different from the meaning of the original verb alone. Phrasal verbs are very common in English, especially in informal speech, and they are a frequent source of questions in JAMB's Lexis section.
A phrase that consists of a verb and a particle (preposition or adverb) which together function as a single verb, often having a meaning that is not obvious from the individual words.
Common Phrasal Verbs and Their Meanings

blocks.caption: Common Phrasal Verbs with Meaning and Example
rows: 'You can <u>look up</u> the word in a dictionary.'
'He <u>brought up</u> an interesting point.' / 'She was <u>brought up</u> in Lagos.'
'It took him a long time to <u>get over</u> the illness.'
'My car <u>broke down</u> on the highway.' / 'She <u>broke down</u> crying.'
'The match was <u>called off</u> due to rain.'

blocks.text: Transitive and Intransitive Phrasal Verbs

items: Transitive: Requires a direct object. (e.g., 'He turned down the offer.' The object is 'the offer'.)
Intransitive: Does not require a direct object. (e.g., 'The car broke down.' No object needed.)

blocks.title: Phrasal Verbs in Context
blocks.text:
• Put off: 'Don't put off your homework until tomorrow.'
  • Turn up: 'I was surprised when he turned up at the party.'
  • Carry out: 'The scientists will carry out the experiment.'

Some phrasal verbs can be separated by their object (e.g., 'turn the offer down'), while others cannot (e.g., 'look after the dog' cannot be 'look the dog after'). This is a nuance that JAMB may test.
Practice Question 1 Select the option that best completes the sentence. 'The government has decided to the new policy until next year.' A. call off B. put off C. turn down D. take up
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Put off' means to postpone or delay. The sentence indicates that the policy will be delayed until next year.
Practice Question 2 Select the option that best completes the sentence. 'I have to my younger sister while my parents are away.' A. look up B. look for C. look after D. look into
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Look after' means to take care of someone. This is the only option that makes sense in the context of taking care of a sister.

lessons.title: Idioms
lessons.summary: A comprehensive look at English idioms, their meanings, and how they are used in context.

blocks.text: An idiom is a group of words that, when used together, have a meaning that is different from the literal meaning of the individual words. They are a colorful and important part of the English language. For JAMB candidates, understanding idioms is crucial, as they are frequently tested in the Lexis and Comprehension sections.
A common expression whose meaning is not predictable from the literal meanings of its constituent words.
Common Idioms and Their Meanings

blocks.caption: Common English Idioms
rows: 'I'm feeling a bit <u>under the weather</u> today.'
'The president <u>hit the nail on the head</u> in his speech.'
'You're about to go on stage? <u>Break a leg</u>!'
'That new phone <u>costs an arm and a leg</u>.'
'Come on, <u>spill the beans</u>! Tell us what happened.'
To do something difficult or unpleasant.
'You'll just have to <u>bite the bullet</u> and face your fears.'
Let the cat out of the bag
'His surprise party was ruined when his sister <u>let the cat out of the bag</u>.'

blocks.text: Idioms in JAMB

JAMB often tests idioms in two ways: 1) Directly asking for the meaning of an idiom in a sentence, or 2) Using an idiom in a comprehension passage and asking for its meaning in context. The key is to know the figurative meaning of the idiom.

blocks.title: Idioms in Context
blocks.text:
• Context: 'The team had to put their heads together to solve the complex problem.' Meaning: To work together as a team to solve something.
  • Context: 'The politician is known for beating around the bush during interviews.' Meaning: To avoid answering a direct question or talking about a main issue.

When learning idioms, focus on the context in which they are used. This is often a better way to remember their meanings than just memorizing a list. Reading widely, especially newspapers and novels, will help you encounter idioms in their natural habitat.

Practice Question 1 What is the meaning of the underlined idiom in the sentence below? 'My uncle has been burning the midnight oil to finish his project.' A. Working late into the night. B. Using a lot of oil. C. Making a fire. D. Sleeping very late.
Correct Answer: A Explanation: The idiom 'burning the midnight oil' means to work or study late into the night.

Practice Question 2 What is the meaning of the underlined idiom in the sentence below? 'When it comes to public speaking, Chidi is a fish out of water.' A. Very relaxed and comfortable. B. Uncomfortable and out of place. C. Very skilled. D. Very messy.
Correct Answer: B Explanation: A 'fish out of water' is a metaphor for someone who is in an unfamiliar or uncomfortable situation.

lessons.title: Word Formation (Prefixes & Suffixes)
lessons.summary: How new words are formed in English through the use of prefixes and suffixes.

blocks.text: Word formation is the process of creating new words from existing ones. In English, this is often done by adding prefixes (at the beginning) or suffixes (at the end) to a root word. Understanding the meaning of common prefixes and suffixes can significantly boost your vocabulary and help you deduce the meaning of unfamiliar words in the JAMB exam.
A word part added to the beginning of a root word to change its meaning. (e.g., un-, re-, pre-, mis-)
A word part added to the end of a root word to change its meaning or its part of speech. (e.g., -ly, -ment, -tion, -able)
Common Prefixes
Common Suffixes

blocks.title: Word Formation in Action
blocks.text:
• Root word: decide (verb)
    • + -tion → decision (noun)
  • Root word: care (noun)
    • + -ful → careful (adjective)
    • + -less → careless (adjective)
    • + -fully → carefully (adverb)
Knowing prefixes and suffixes is a powerful vocabulary-building tool. It can help you decode the meaning of a long, unfamiliar word by breaking it down into its parts.
Practice Question 1 The word 'illegible' can be formed from which root word and prefix? A. legible + il- B. legible + un- C. legal + il- D. legible + in-

Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Illegible' means not clear enough to read. It is formed from the root word 'legible' (readable) and the prefix 'il-', which means 'not'. The 'il-' prefix is used before words that start with 'l'.
Practice Question 2 Which of the following words is formed by adding a suffix to the word 'manage'? A. Mismanage B. Management C. Manager D. Both B and C
Correct Answer: D Explanation: 'Management' adds the suffix '-ment' (manage + -ment). 'Manager' adds the suffix '-er' (manage + -er). 'Mismanage' adds a prefix ('mis-'), not a suffix.

lessons.title: Common Grammatical Errors
lessons.summary: A review of the most common grammatical errors tested in JAMB, including misplaced modifiers, faulty parallelism, and double negatives.

blocks.text: In addition to specific rules, JAMB often tests your ability to identify and correct common grammatical errors. These questions are designed to see if you have a good command of standard English. This lesson covers some of the most frequent pitfalls for candidates.
Error 1: Misplaced Modifiers

A modifier is a word, phrase, or clause that describes (modifies) another word in the sentence. A misplaced modifier is placed too far from the word it is supposed to describe, leading to confusion or a humorous meaning.

blocks.title: Misplaced Modifier
blocks.text:
• Confusing: 'The man was walking his dog in a red shirt.' (Is the man or the dog in the red shirt?)
  • Corrected: 'The man in a red shirt was walking his dog.'
Error 2: Faulty Parallelism
Parallelism means using the same grammatical structure for items in a list or comparison. When the items are not balanced, it creates faulty parallelism.

blocks.title: Faulty Parallelism
blocks.text:
• Faulty: 'She likes swimming, to run, and reading.' (swimming (gerund), to run (infinitive), reading (gerund))
  • Corrected: 'She likes swimming, running, and reading.' (All gerunds) OR 'She likes to swim, to run, and to read.' (All infinitives)
Error 3: Double Negatives
A double negative occurs when two negative words are used in the same clause. In standard English, this is considered an error (except in some dialects). It creates a positive meaning by accident.

blocks.title: Double Negative
blocks.text:
• Incorrect: 'I don't have no money.' (Meaning: I have money? Or I don't have money?)
  • Corrected: 'I don't have any money.' OR 'I have no money.'
Error 4: Misuse of 'Me' and 'I'
Students often confuse the subjective ('I') and objective ('me') cases, especially in compound subjects or objects.

blocks.title: Me vs. I
blocks.text:
• Incorrect (as subject): 'Me and my friend went to the market.' (Subject should be 'My friend and I')
  • Correct: 'My friend and I went to the market.'
  • Incorrect (as object): 'The gift was for my wife and I.' (Object of preposition 'for' should be 'me')
  • Correct: 'The gift was for my wife and me.'
A word or phrase that is placed too far from the word it modifies, making the sentence confusing.

Practice Question 1 Identify the error in the following sentence. 'We saw a large collection of books at the library that were very old.' A. The subject is missing. B. There is a misplaced modifier. C. There is a faulty parallelism. D. The sentence is correct as is.

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The phrase 'that were very old' is a misplaced modifier. It is placed next to 'library,' suggesting the library is old. It should be placed next to 'books' to be correct: 'We saw a large collection of books that were very old at the library.'

Practice Question 2 Identify the error in the following sentence. 'He said he didn't know nothing about the incident.' A. Misplaced modifier. B. Faulty parallelism. C. Double negative. D. Wrong preposition.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The sentence contains a double negative: 'didn't know nothing.' The correct form is 'didn't know anything' or 'knew nothing'.

lessons.title: Synonyms
lessons.summary: Understanding synonyms, their use, and how to choose the best synonym in context.

blocks.text: A synonym is a word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word. Synonyms are important for expanding vocabulary and for answering questions that ask for the closest meaning. However, synonyms often have different connotations, so choosing the correct one depends on context.
Example Synonyms
Context is Key

Not all synonyms are interchangeable. For example, 'childish' and 'childlike' are synonyms but have different connotations (childish is negative, childlike is positive). JAMB may test your ability to choose the most appropriate synonym for a given context.
Practice Question Choose the best synonym for 'courageous' as used in the sentence: 'The courageous firefighter saved the child.' A. Foolhardy B. Brave C. Reckless D. Careless
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Brave' is a direct synonym for courageous. 'Foolhardy' and 'reckless' imply a lack of caution, which is not suggested by the context.

lessons.title: Antonyms
lessons.summary: Understanding antonyms, words with opposite meanings, and how they are tested.

blocks.text: An antonym is a word that has the opposite meaning of another word. Antonyms are common in vocabulary tests, and recognizing them helps in understanding text and answering questions about contrast.
Examples of Antonyms
Practice Question Which of the following is the antonym of 'temporary'? A. Short-lived B. Permanent C. Brief D. Transient
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Permanent' means lasting forever, which is the opposite of 'temporary' (lasting for a limited time).

lessons.title: Homonyms, Homophones, and Homographs
lessons.summary: Distinguishing between words that sound alike, look alike, or are spelled alike.

blocks.text: These terms are often confused. Homonyms are words that sound alike but have different meanings and spellings (e.g., 'sea' and 'see') – also called homophones. Homophones are words that sound the same but are spelled differently and have different meanings. Homographs are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings and may have different pronunciations (e.g., 'tear' as in crying vs. 'tear' as in rip). JAMB may test your ability to choose the correct word based on context.

blocks.caption: Examples
rows: Same sound, different spelling and meaning.
Same spelling, different meaning (and sometimes pronunciation).

blocks.text: Practice Question Which of the following pairs are homophones? A. 'Bare' and 'bear' B. 'Read' (present) and 'read' (past) C. 'Lead' (metal) and 'lead' (to guide) D. 'Desert' (dry land) and 'desert' (abandon)
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Bare' (naked) and 'bear' (animal) sound the same but are spelled differently. The others are homographs (same spelling, different meanings).

lessons.title: Clauses
lessons.summary: A detailed look at independent and dependent clauses, including relative, adverbial, and noun clauses.

blocks.text: A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a verb. Clauses can be independent (able to stand alone) or dependent (cannot stand alone). Understanding clauses is essential for sentence structure and punctuation.
Independent Clauses
An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence. (e.g., 'She went to the store.')
Dependent Clauses
A dependent clause cannot stand alone; it must be attached to an independent clause. Types include:

items: Noun Clause: Acts as a noun (e.g., 'What she said surprised me.').
Adjective (Relative) Clause: Modifies a noun (e.g., 'The man who came is my uncle.').
Adverbial Clause: Modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb (e.g., 'He left because he was tired.').

blocks.text: Practice Question Identify the type of clause underlined in the sentence: 'Although it was raining, we went for a walk.' A. Noun clause B. Adjective clause C. Adverbial clause D. Independent clause
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The clause 'Although it was raining' modifies the verb 'went' by giving context (concession), so it is an adverbial clause.

lessons.title: Sentence Patterns
lessons.summary: Common English sentence patterns: subject-verb, subject-verb-object, and others.

blocks.text: Sentence patterns refer to the basic grammatical structures of sentences. Recognizing patterns helps in constructing correct sentences and in understanding sentence meaning. The most common patterns are:

items: SV (Subject + Verb): 'Birds fly.'
SVO (Subject + Verb + Object): 'She reads books.'
SVC (Subject + Verb + Complement): 'He is a doctor.'
SVOO (Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object): 'She gave him a gift.'
SVOC (Subject + Verb + Object + Complement): 'They elected him president.'

blocks.text: Practice Question What sentence pattern is used in 'The teacher gave the students a test'? A. SV B. SVO C. SVOO D. SVOC
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Teacher' (S), 'gave' (V), 'students' (Indirect Object), 'test' (Direct Object). This is SVOO.

lessons.title: Mood (Indicative, Imperative, Subjunctive)
lessons.summary: Understanding the three moods of verbs and their usage.

blocks.text: Mood in grammar indicates the attitude of the speaker towards the action. There are three main moods: indicative (fact), imperative (command), and subjunctive (hypothetical or wish). The subjunctive is often tested in JAMB.
Indicative Mood
States facts, opinions, or questions. (e.g., 'The sun rises in the east.')
Imperative Mood
Expresses a command or request. (e.g., 'Close the door.')
Subjunctive Mood

Expresses hypothetical situations, wishes, or conditions contrary to fact. Often uses 'were' for all subjects and 'that' clauses. (e.g., 'If I were rich, I would travel.', 'I wish he were here.', 'It is essential that he be present.')
Practice Question Which mood is used in the sentence 'If I were you, I would apologize'? A. Indicative B. Imperative C. Subjunctive D. Interrogative
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The use of 'were' with 'I' indicates a subjunctive mood, expressing an unreal condition.

lessons.title: Aspect
lessons.summary: Understanding verb aspect: simple, progressive, perfect, and perfect progressive.

blocks.text: Aspect indicates whether an action is completed, ongoing, or repeated. It is combined with tense to form verb phrases. The four aspects are: simple, progressive, perfect, and perfect progressive.

blocks.caption: Aspects with Examples
rows: Completed action with relevance to another time.
Ongoing action that started in the past and continues.

blocks.text: Practice Question Which aspect is used in 'They have been waiting for an hour'? A. Simple B. Progressive C. Perfect D. Perfect Progressive
Correct Answer: D Explanation: The verb phrase 'have been waiting' indicates an ongoing action that started in the past and continues, which is perfect progressive.

lessons.title: Number (Singular/Plural)
lessons.summary: Understanding singular and plural forms of nouns and their agreement with verbs.

blocks.text: Number refers to the grammatical category of singular or plural. It applies mainly to nouns and pronouns, and determines verb agreement. Irregular plurals and special cases are common JAMB traps.
Regular Plurals
Most nouns add -s or -es. (e.g., cat → cats, box → boxes)
Irregular Plurals
Some nouns change form (e.g., child → children, mouse → mice). Others remain the same (e.g., sheep, deer).
Practice Question What is the plural of 'crisis'? A. Crisises B. Crises C. Crisi D. Crisis
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Crisis' is a Greek-derived word; its plural is 'crises'.

lessons.title: Concord (Advanced)
lessons.summary: Advanced and exceptional rules of subject-verb agreement, including tricky cases and common JAMB traps.

blocks.text: While basic subject-verb agreement (2.7) covers the main rules, this lesson delves into advanced and exceptional cases that frequently appear in JAMB. Mastering these will help you tackle the most difficult agreement questions.
Special Cases

items: Subject preceded by 'each' or 'every': These make the subject singular. (e.g., 'Each of the students is responsible.')
Compound subjects with 'and' but referring to one thing: (e.g., 'Bread and butter is my breakfast.')
Collective nouns acting individually: (e.g., 'The staff are debating among themselves.')
Indefinite pronouns like 'none': 'None' can be singular or plural depending on context. (e.g., 'None of the money was found.' vs. 'None of the students were present.')
Subject with 'more than one': Usually singular. (e.g., 'More than one student has complained.')
Subject with 'a number of' vs. 'the number of': 'A number of' is plural; 'the number of' is singular. (e.g., 'A number of issues have arisen. The number of issues is growing.')

blocks.text: Practice Question Select the correct verb. 'A number of students complaining about the new policy.' A. is B. are
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'A number of' is a plural expression, so the verb should be plural: 'are'.

lessons.title: Degrees of Comparison
lessons.summary: Understanding positive, comparative, and superlative degrees of adjectives and adverbs.

blocks.text: Degrees of comparison are used to compare the qualities of people, things, or actions. There are three degrees: positive (basic form), comparative (comparing two), and superlative (comparing three or more).
Practice Question What is the superlative form of 'intelligent'? A. More intelligent B. Most intelligent C. Intelligenter D. Inteligentest
Correct Answer: B Explanation: For longer adjectives, the superlative is formed with 'most' + adjective.

lessons.title: Mechanics
lessons.summary: Capitalization, abbreviation, and other mechanical conventions in English.

blocks.text: Mechanics refers to the conventions of written English, including capitalization, abbreviation, numbers, and italics. JAMB may test your knowledge of correct capitalization and abbreviation rules.
Capitalization Rules

items: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence.
Capitalize proper nouns (names of people, places, organizations, etc.).
Capitalize days, months, and holidays, but not seasons.
Capitalize titles when they precede a name (e.g., President Buhari).
Capitalize the first letter of each major word in titles of books, articles, etc.

blocks.text: Practice Question Which of the following is correctly capitalized? A. I visited lagos last week. B. She is studying at the university of lagos. C. The book is titled 'Things fall Apart'. D. He was born in October.
Correct Answer: D Explanation: Months are always capitalized. Options A, B, and C have errors in proper noun capitalization (Lagos, University of Lagos, Things Fall Apart).

lessons.title: Punctuation
lessons.summary: A guide to the correct use of punctuation marks: commas, full stops, apostrophes, etc.

blocks.text: Punctuation marks are essential for clarity and meaning. Common punctuation marks tested in JAMB include the comma, full stop, apostrophe, semicolon, colon, and quotation marks.
Key Rules

items: Full stop (.): Ends a declarative sentence.
Comma (,): Separates items in a list, clauses, and non-essential elements.
Apostrophe ('): Indicates possession or omission (contractions).
Semicolon (;): Links closely related independent clauses.
Colon (:): Introduces a list, explanation, or quotation.
Quotation marks ("..."): Enclose direct speech or titles.

blocks.title: Common Errors
blocks.text:
• Incorrect: 'Its a beautiful day.' Correct: 'It's a beautiful day.' (apostrophe for contraction)
  • Incorrect: 'The students' books, are on the table.' Correct: 'The students' books are on the table.' (no comma after books)
Practice Question Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly? A. The dog wagged its tail. B. The dog wagged it's tail. C. The dog wagged its' tail. D. The dog wagged it's tail.
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Its' is the possessive form; 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is'. The correct possessive is 'its' without an apostrophe.

lessons.title: Spelling
lessons.summary: Common spelling rules, irregular spellings, and frequently misspelled words.

blocks.text: Spelling is often tested in JAMB through error identification or fill-in-the-blank. Memorizing common spelling rules and frequently misspelled words is helpful.
Common Spelling Rules

items: i before e except after c (e.g., believe, receive).
Drop the final 'e' before adding a suffix starting with a vowel (e.g., hope → hoping).
Double the final consonant when adding -ed or -ing if the word ends in consonant-vowel-consonant and the stress is on the last syllable (e.g., stop → stopping).

blocks.text: Frequently Misspelled Words
Practice Question Choose the correct spelling. A. Indispensable B. Indispensible C. Indispensible D. Indispensable
Correct Answer: A Explanation: The correct spelling is 'indispensable'.

lessons.title: Ordinary Usage
lessons.summary: The everyday meaning and use of common words in context.

blocks.text: Ordinary usage refers to the standard, everyday meanings of words, as opposed to specialized or figurative meanings. JAMB may test your knowledge of the common definitions of words in sentences.
Practice Question What is the ordinary meaning of 'restrain'? A. To encourage B. To hold back C. To release D. To ignore
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Restrain' means to hold back or prevent someone from doing something.

lessons.title: Figurative Usage
lessons.summary: Understanding the figurative (non-literal) meanings of words and phrases.

blocks.text: Figurative usage involves using words in a non-literal way to create a particular effect, such as metaphor, simile, or personification. JAMB may ask you to interpret the figurative meaning of a word or phrase in a sentence.

blocks.title: Figurative vs. Literal
blocks.text:
• Literal: 'The sun is bright.'
  • Figurative: 'She is the sun of my life.' (meaning she brings light and warmth, not literally a star)

Practice Question In the sentence 'He has a heart of stone,' what is the figurative meaning of 'stone'? A. Hard and unemotional B. Solid and reliable C. Precious and valuable D. Cold and uncomfortable
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Heart of stone' figuratively means lacking compassion or being unemotional.

lessons.title: Idiomatic Usage
lessons.summary: Common idiomatic expressions and their correct usage in sentences.

blocks.text: Idiomatic usage refers to expressions that are not literal but have a conventional meaning. JAMB often tests idioms in sentence completion or error identification. Knowing the correct form and meaning of common idioms is essential.
Common Idiomatic Errors

items: Incorrect: 'She is very good in mathematics.' Correct: 'She is very good at mathematics.'
Incorrect: 'He insisted to come.' Correct: 'He insisted on coming.'
Incorrect: 'The committee is made of ten members.' Correct: 'The committee is made up of ten members.'

blocks.text: Practice Question Choose the correct idiomatic expression. 'The manager was angry ___ the employees for the error.' A. on B. at C. with D. about
Correct Answer: C Explanation: The correct idiom is 'angry with' when referring to a person.

lessons.title: Sentence Interpretation
lessons.summary: How to interpret the meaning of a sentence, including implied meaning and nuance.

blocks.text: Sentence interpretation questions test your ability to understand what a sentence means, including the implied meaning or the speaker's attitude. It often involves identifying the correct paraphrase or the best explanation of the sentence.

blocks.title: Interpretation Example
blocks.text:
Sentence: 'I didn't mean to hurt you.'

Interpretation: The speaker apologizes for causing pain, but did not intend it.

Practice Question What does the sentence 'He is not the most hardworking person I know' imply? A. He is the least hardworking. B. He is very hardworking. C. He is not as hardworking as some others. D. He is average.
Correct Answer: C Explanation: This is a form of litotes; it implies he is not among the top hardworking people, but not necessarily the worst.

lessons.title: Sentence Completion
lessons.summary: Strategies for completing sentences with the correct word or phrase.

blocks.text: Sentence completion questions require you to choose the best word or phrase to fill a blank. These test your vocabulary, grammar, and ability to understand context. Strategies include:

items: Read the entire sentence to understand the context.
Look for clues in the rest of the sentence (e.g., cause-effect, contrast).
Determine the part of speech needed.
Eliminate options that do not fit grammatically or meaningfully.

blocks.text: Practice Question Complete the sentence: 'Despite his ______, he managed to win the competition.' A. talent B. experience C. injury D. training
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Despite' indicates a contrast; an injury would be a disadvantage that makes his victory more impressive.

lessons.title: Error Identification
lessons.summary: How to spot grammatical errors in sentences, including common traps.

blocks.text: In error identification questions, you must find the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error. This tests your knowledge of all the rules covered earlier. Strategies include:

items: Check subject-verb agreement.
Check tense consistency.
Check pronoun case and agreement.
Check prepositions and idioms.
Check modifiers and parallelism.
Read the sentence aloud to hear if it sounds wrong.

blocks.text: Practice Question Identify the error in the sentence: 'Neither the manager nor his assistants was present at the meeting.' A. Neither B. nor C. assistants D. was
Correct Answer: D Explanation: With 'nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject ('assistants' is plural), so it should be 'were', not 'was'.

lessons.title: Lexis and Structure Revision
lessons.summary: A concise summary of the key rules and concepts from the Lexis and Structure section.

blocks.text: Key Grammatical Rules Summary

items: Parts of Speech: Identify the function of words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, etc.) in a sentence.
Tenses: Use the correct tense to show the time of an action (present, past, future). Pay special attention to the perfect and continuous forms.
Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. Beware of tricky subjects like 'each,' 'everyone,' and collective nouns.
Question Tags: A positive statement takes a negative tag and vice versa. Remember the special cases like 'aren't I?' and 'shall we?'.
Conditionals: Know the four types (zero, first, second, third) and the correct tense patterns for each.
Reported Speech: Remember to change pronouns, tense, and time expressions when reporting what someone said.
Active and Passive Voice: In active voice, the subject does the action; in passive voice, the subject receives the action.
Prepositions: Use the correct preposition to show relationships of time, place, and direction.
Conjunctions: Use the correct connector ('and,' 'but,' 'because,' 'although,' etc.) to join ideas.

blocks.text: Key Vocabulary Concepts Summary

items: Synonyms and Antonyms: Words with similar and opposite meanings.
Phrasal Verbs: Verbs combined with particles (e.g., look up, give up).
Idioms: Expressions with figurative meanings (e.g., piece of cake, under the weather).
Word Formation: How prefixes and suffixes change the meaning and part of speech of words.

blocks.text: Examination Reminders

items: Read the question carefully. Identify if it's testing a tense rule, a pronoun case, a preposition, or vocabulary.
Eliminate the most obvious wrong answers first.
Watch out for traps like the 'one-word' error in a sentence.
Trust your knowledge of the rules. If a sentence 'sounds' wrong, it probably is.
For vocabulary questions, always consider the context of the sentence.

blocks.text: Regular practice with JAMB-style questions is the most effective way to master Lexis and Structure. The more you practice, the more comfortable you will become with identifying and applying these rules.

lessons.title: Full JAMB Lexis & Structure Practice
lessons.summary: A comprehensive set of practice questions covering all Lexis and Structure topics.

blocks.text: Test your overall knowledge with these mixed questions. Choose the best option for each.
1. Choose the correct verb form: 'The committee ______ divided on the issue.' A. is B. are C. was D. were
Answer: B or D (are/were) Explanation: Here the committee members are acting as individuals, so plural verb is required.
2. Choose the correct question tag: 'You have finished, ______?' A. haven't you B. have you C. didn't you D. don't you
Answer: A Explanation: Positive statement takes negative tag: haven't you.
3. Identify the error: 'She is more taller than her sister.' A. more B. taller C. than D. sister
Answer: A Explanation: 'More' is redundant with 'taller' (comparative already). Correct: 'She is taller than her sister.'
4. Choose the correct preposition: 'He is good ______ mathematics.' A. in B. at C. on D. for
Answer: B Explanation: The idiom is 'good at'.
5. What is the synonym of 'enormous'? A. small B. huge C. tiny D. medium
Answer: B Explanation: 'Enormous' means very large, synonym is 'huge'.

lessons.title: Introduction to Oral Forms
lessons.summary: An overview of the Oral English section, focusing on the sounds of English and how they are tested in JAMB.

blocks.text: The Oral English section of JAMB tests your knowledge of English pronunciation. It does not test your own speaking ability, but rather your ability to identify the correct pronunciation of words and sounds. This section is often found challenging by candidates because it requires a good ear for the different sounds of English.
Why is Oral English Important?

items: A specific section of the JAMB Use of English exam is dedicated to it.
It tests your understanding of the sounds of English, which is crucial for clear communication.
It helps you avoid pronunciation errors that can affect your spoken English and comprehension.

blocks.text: To do well in this section, you need to understand the fundamental concepts of English phonetics, including vowels, consonants, stress, and intonation. This section of the textbook will guide you through these concepts.
The study of the physical sounds of human speech.

To practice for the Oral English section, you can listen to audio from reputable English dictionaries (like the BBC or Merriam-Webster) to hear the correct pronunciations of words. Reading aloud carefully and paying attention to how different sounds are formed in your mouth can also be helpful.

lessons.title: Monophthongs
lessons.summary: A detailed look at pure vowel sounds (monophthongs) with examples and pronunciation guidance.

blocks.text: A monophthong is a vowel sound that has a single, unchanging sound quality throughout its duration. English has 12 monophthongs (though some may vary by accent). These are also called pure vowels.
Practice Question Which word has the /iː/ sound? A. Ship B. Sheep C. Shape D. Chop
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Sheep' has the long /iː/ sound. 'Ship' has /ɪ/, 'Shape' has /eɪ/, 'Chop' has /ɒ/.

lessons.title: Diphthongs
lessons.summary: An explanation of diphthongs—vowel sounds that glide from one quality to another.

blocks.text: A diphthong is a vowel sound that involves a change in quality, a glide from one vowel to another within the same syllable. English has eight common diphthongs.
Practice Question Which word contains the /aɪ/ diphthong? A. Now B. Know C. Noise D. Night
Correct Answer: D Explanation: 'Night' is pronounced /naɪt/ with the /aɪ/ sound. 'Now' is /aʊ/, 'Know' is /əʊ/, 'Noise' is /ɔɪ/.

lessons.title: Triphthongs
lessons.summary: Extended explanation of triphthongs—vowel sounds that glide through three qualities.

blocks.text: A triphthong is a complex vowel sound that glides through three different vowel qualities in a single syllable. In English, triphthongs are often formed by adding the schwa /ə/ to a diphthong. Common examples include /aɪə/ (as in 'fire'), /aʊə/ (as in 'hour'), and /əʊə/ (as in 'lower'). These are less common but may appear in JAMB.
Practice Question Which of the following words contains a triphthong? A. Beer B. Power C. Say D. Boy
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Power' is pronounced /paʊə/, which contains the triphthong /aʊə/.

lessons.title: Consonants and Consonant Sounds
lessons.summary: An introduction to consonant sounds, their classification, and common contrasts.

blocks.text: A consonant is a speech sound produced by partially or completely blocking the flow of air as it passes through the vocal tract. Unlike vowels, which have a clear, open sound, consonants involve some obstruction or friction. Understanding the different consonant sounds is essential for Oral English questions.
Consonant Sounds

Consonant sounds are classified by their place of articulation (where the obstruction happens) and manner of articulation (how the obstruction happens). For JAMB purposes, it is most important to know the basic sounds and their symbols.

blocks.caption: Common Consonant Sounds with Word Examples

blocks.text: Common Consonant Contrasts
JAMB often tests your ability to distinguish between similar consonant sounds, especially those that are easily confused by Nigerian speakers. Here are some common contrasts.

blocks.caption: Common Consonant Contrasts
rows: 'shin' vs. 'gin' (the sound /ʒ/ is the 'zh' sound, rare in English but common in words like 'vision').

blocks.text: A speech sound that is produced with partial or complete obstruction of the airflow.
Practice Question 1 Which of the following words begins with a different consonant sound? A. Thin B. That C. Think D. Thick
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'That' begins with the voiced /ð/ sound. 'Thin,' 'Think,' and 'Thick' all begin with the voiceless /θ/ sound.

lessons.title: Consonant Clusters
lessons.summary: Understanding sequences of two or more consonants without intervening vowels.

blocks.text: A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds that appear together without a vowel between them. Examples: 'str' in 'street', 'spl' in 'split', 'nds' in 'bends'. JAMB may test recognition or pronunciation of clusters, especially those that are challenging for Nigerian English speakers.
Common Clusters

items: Initial clusters: 'pl', 'br', 'tr', 'sk', 'sp', 'str', 'spl', 'spr'.
Final clusters: '-nt', '-mp', '-nd', '-sk', '-st', '-ld', '-nth', '-ths'.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.text:
• 'split' has /spl/ cluster.
  • 'glimpse' has /mps/ cluster.
  • 'strengths' has /ŋkθs/ cluster—a difficult one.
Practice Question Which word has a consonant cluster at the beginning? A. Pencil B. Spin C. End D. Ink
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Spin' begins with the cluster /sp/. 'Pencil' begins with /p/, 'End' and 'Ink' start with vowels.

lessons.title: Rhymes
lessons.summary: An explanation of rhymes and how to identify rhyming words in the Oral English section.

blocks.text: A rhyme is a repetition of similar sounds in two or more words, usually at the end of the words (in poetry or lyrics) but can also be internal. In the JAMB Oral English section, you will be asked to identify which word does not rhyme with the others or which pair of words rhyme. This tests your ability to identify the exact vowel and consonant sounds at the end of words.
The correspondence of sound between words, especially at the end of the words.
How to Identify a Rhyme
For two words to rhyme, they must have the same vowel sound and the same final consonant sound (if any). The initial consonant sound(s) can be different.

blocks.title: Identifying Rhymes
blocks.text:
• Cat / Hat: They rhyme. Both have the /æ/ and /t/ sound (c-æ-t, h-æ-t).
  • Dog / Log: They rhyme. Both have the /ɒ/ and /g/ sound (d-ɒ-g, l-ɒ-g).
  • Bite / Night: They rhyme. Both have the /aɪ/ and /t/ sound (b-aɪ-t, n-aɪ-t).
  • Sing / Ring: They rhyme. Both have the /ɪ/ and /ŋ/ sound (s-ɪ-ŋ, r-ɪ-ŋ).
  • Chair / Care: They rhyme. Both have the /eə/ sound (ch-eə, c-eə).

Be careful! Words may be spelled similarly but have different pronunciations and therefore do not rhyme. The key is the sound, not the spelling. Example: 'Bough' (pronounced bow) and 'Rough' (pronounced ruff) do not rhyme, even though they look like they might.
Practice Question Which word does not rhyme with the others? A. Know B. How C. Now D. Cow
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Know' is pronounced /nəʊ/. 'How,' 'Now,' and 'Cow' are all pronounced with the /aʊ/ sound. Therefore, 'Know' does not rhyme.

lessons.title: Homophones
lessons.summary: Understanding words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.

blocks.text: Homophones are words that are pronounced the same but have different meanings and often different spellings. In Oral English, you may be asked to identify homophones or to distinguish them in context.
Practice Question Which pair is a homophone? A. 'Read' and 'red' B. 'Read' (present) and 'read' (past) C. 'Live' (alive) and 'live' (reside) D. 'Tear' (rip) and 'tear' (eye drop)
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Read' (present tense) and 'red' (color) sound the same (/rɛd/). The others are homographs (same spelling) or have different pronunciations.

lessons.title: Word Stress
lessons.summary: A guide to understanding and identifying word stress patterns in English.

blocks.text: Word stress is the emphasis placed on a particular syllable in a word. In English, not all syllables in a word are pronounced with the same force. The stressed syllable is louder, longer, and has a higher pitch. Stressing the wrong syllable can change the meaning of a word or make it difficult to understand. Word stress is a common area tested in JAMB Oral English.
A unit of sound containing a vowel sound. A word can have one or more syllables. (e.g., 'cat' has 1 syllable, 'water' has 2, 'beautiful' has 3).
Rules and Patterns

items: Two-syllable nouns: stress often on the first syllable.
Two-syllable verbs: stress often on the second syllable.
Compound nouns: stress on the first part.
Words ending in -tion, -sion: stress on the syllable before the suffix.

blocks.text: Practice Question Which syllable is stressed in 'communication'? A. First B. Second C. Third D. Fourth
Correct Answer: D Explanation: The stress is on the fourth syllable (the one before '-tion'): com-mu-ni-'CA-tion.

lessons.title: Monosyllabic Stress
lessons.summary: Stress in one-syllable words—usually every syllable is stressed, but focus on vowel quality.

blocks.text: In monosyllabic (one-syllable) words, the stress is naturally on that single syllable. However, the vowel sound is often pronounced with full quality (not reduced). JAMB may test the correct vowel sound rather than stress placement, as there is no choice.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.text: Words like 'cat', 'dog', 'sun', 'book' have stress on the only syllable. The vowel sound is distinct.
Practice Question Which of the following is a monosyllabic word? A. Beautiful B. Elephant C. Cat D. Water
Correct Answer: C Explanation: 'Cat' has one syllable; the others have multiple.

lessons.title: Disyllabic Stress
lessons.summary: Stress patterns in two-syllable words, with attention to noun-verb shifts.

blocks.text: In disyllabic (two-syllable) words, stress often falls on the first syllable for nouns and adjectives, and on the second syllable for verbs. However, there are many exceptions.
Practice Question How is the noun 'permit' stressed? A. per'MIT B. 'PERmit C. PER'mit D. per'MIT
Correct Answer: B Explanation: The noun 'permit' has stress on the first syllable: 'PERmit.'

lessons.title: Polysyllabic Stress
lessons.summary: Stress patterns in words with three or more syllables, focusing on common rules.

blocks.text: In polysyllabic (three or more syllables) words, stress is often determined by suffixes. For instance, words ending in '-tion', '-sion', '-ic', '-ical', '-ity' usually have stress on the syllable immediately before the suffix.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.text:
• 'edu'CA'tion' (before -tion)
  • 'e'LEc'tric' (before -ic)
  • 'po'LI'tical' (before -ical)
  • 'e'LEc'tricity' (before -ity)
Practice Question Where is the stress in 'democracy'? A. First syllable B. Second syllable C. Third syllable D. Fourth syllable
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'democracy' has stress on the second syllable: de'mo'cra'cy? Actually, it's de'MOCracy, stress on the second syllable. So B.

lessons.title: Stress Shifts
lessons.summary: How stress can shift when a word changes form (noun to verb, or with suffixes).

blocks.text: Stress shifts occur when a word changes its part of speech or when suffixes are added. For example, 'photograph' (noun) stress on first syllable; 'photographer' stress on second syllable; 'photographic' stress on third syllable. JAMB may test these shifts.
Practice Question What is the stress pattern in 'photographer'? A. First syllable B. Second syllable C. Third syllable D. Fourth syllable
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'photographer' has stress on the second syllable: pho-'TO-gra-pher.

lessons.title: Sentence / Emphatic Stress
lessons.summary: An explanation of emphatic stress and how it changes meaning in a sentence.

blocks.text: Emphatic stress is the additional emphasis placed on a particular word within a sentence to highlight its importance or to contrast it with another idea. Unlike word stress (which is about syllables), emphatic stress is about the entire word. By changing the word that is stressed, you can change the entire meaning of the sentence.
The particular emphasis placed on a word in a sentence to indicate its importance, to contrast it, or to answer a specific question.

blocks.title: Emphatic Stress Changing Meaning
blocks.text:
Consider the sentence: 'I told him to come.' The meaning changes depending on the word you stress.
  • 'I' told him to come. (Emphasis on the speaker, not someone else.)
  • I 'told' him to come. (Emphasis on the act of telling, not something else.)
  • I told 'him' to come. (Emphasis on the person told, not someone else.)
  • I told him to 'come'. (Emphasis on the action, not something else like 'go' or 'stay'.)
How Emphatic Stress is Tested in JAMB

In JAMB, you will be given a sentence with a stressed word, and you will be asked to identify the question that the sentence would be a correct answer to. The stressed word is the focus of the question.

blocks.title: JAMB-Style Emphatic Stress Question
blocks.text: If the sentence is: 'The student BORROWED the book from the library.' This sentence would be a suitable answer to the question: 'What did the student do to the book?' (Answer: He borrowed it, not bought it or stole it).

Practice Question If the sentence 'The manager PROMOTED Ahmed to a new position' is given with emphasis on 'promoted,' what question is it likely answering? A. Who promoted Ahmed? B. What did the manager do to Ahmed? C. Who was promoted? D. When was Ahmed promoted?

Correct Answer: B Explanation: The emphasis is on the action ('promoted'). Therefore, the question it answers is about what the manager did. Options A, C, and D would require emphasis on 'manager,' 'Ahmed,' and a time word, respectively.

lessons.title: Intonation
lessons.summary: Understanding rising and falling tones in English speech and their meanings.

blocks.text: Intonation refers to the rise and fall of pitch in speech. It can change the meaning of a sentence, indicating whether it is a statement, question, or expresses emotion. JAMB may test your understanding of intonation patterns, especially in question tags and sentence types.
Common Patterns

items: Falling intonation: Used in statements, commands, and wh-questions (e.g., 'You are coming. (fall)' )
Rising intonation: Used in yes/no questions (e.g., 'Are you coming? (rise)' )
Rise-fall: Expresses surprise or emphasis.

blocks.text: Practice Question Which intonation pattern is typical for a wh-question like 'What is your name?'? A. Rising B. Falling C. Rise-fall D. Level
Correct Answer: B Explanation: Wh-questions usually have falling intonation.

lessons.title: Silent Letters
lessons.summary: Common silent letters in English and how they affect pronunciation.

blocks.text: Silent letters are letters that appear in spelling but are not pronounced. They are common in English and can be tricky. JAMB may test your awareness of silent letters through pronunciation questions.
Practice Question Which word has a silent letter? A. Cat B. Knife C. Dog D. Sun
Correct Answer: B Explanation: 'Knife' has a silent 'k'.

lessons.title: Common Pronunciation Traps
lessons.summary: Commonly mispronounced words and typical traps in JAMB Oral English.

blocks.text: Some words are frequently mispronounced by Nigerian students. Pay attention to vowel sounds, silent letters, and stress. Common traps include:

items: Vowel length: 'sheep' vs. 'ship'
Consonant sounds: 'think' vs. 'sink' (θ vs. s)
Stress shift: 'present' (noun) vs. 'present' (verb)
Silent letters: 'hour' (h silent), 'knock' (k silent)
Words with 'ough': 'though' (əʊ), 'through' (uː), 'tough' (ʌf), 'cough' (ɒf)

blocks.text: Practice Question Which word is often mispronounced as having a short vowel? A. Sheep B. Ship C. Shape D. Shop
Correct Answer: A Explanation: 'Sheep' has the long /iː/ sound, but some may pronounce it like 'ship' /ɪ/.

lessons.title: Oral English JAMB Practice
lessons.summary: A set of practice questions covering all Oral English topics.

blocks.text: Test your knowledge with these practice questions.
1. Which of the following words has the /iː/ sound? A. Sin B. Seen C. Sun D. Son
Answer: B Explanation: 'Seen' has the long /iː/.
2. Which word rhymes with 'know'? A. Now B. How C. Cow D. Go
Answer: D Explanation: 'Go' and 'know' rhyme with /əʊ/.
3. Where is the stress in 'photographic'? A. First B. Second C. Third D. Fourth

Answer: C Explanation: 'photographic' stress on third syllable: pho-to-'GRA-phic? Actually, it's on the third: pho-to-'GRA-phic? The stress is on the second? Let's correct: 'photographic' stress is on the second? Actually, it's pho-to-'GRA-phic? I think it's on the 'graph' syllable which is third? Let's check: pho-to-GRA-phi? Actually, common pronunciation: /ˌfoʊtəˈɡræfɪk/ stress on 'graf' which is the third syllable? We'll just say it's on the third syllable.
4. Which has a silent 'k'? A. Kick B. Knee C. Keep D. Kill
Answer: B Explanation: 'Knee' has silent 'k'.

lessons.title: Oral English Revision
lessons.summary: A concise summary of key concepts in Oral English.

blocks.text: Key Sounds Summary
Key Stress Concepts Summary

items: Word Stress: Emphasis on a specific syllable; often predictable by word class or suffixes.
Emphatic Stress: Emphasis on a specific word to change meaning; tested by identifying the question it answers.

blocks.text: Examination Reminders

items: For vowel questions, focus on sound, not spelling.
For consonant questions, pay close attention to articulation (e.g., /θ/ vs. /ð/).
For word stress, memorize common patterns and practice with a dictionary.
For emphatic stress, identify the stressed word and think about what question it would answer.
For rhyme, focus on the final vowel and consonant sounds.

blocks.text: Oral English can be mastered through consistent practice. Use online dictionaries that provide audio pronunciations and listen carefully to the sounds.

lessons.title: Prescribed Reading Text Introduction
lessons.summary: An introduction to the prescribed reading text section, its importance, and how to study it.

blocks.text: The Prescribed Reading Text section of JAMB Use of English tests your knowledge and understanding of a specific literary text set by the examination board. This section requires you to have read and studied the text in detail. You will be asked questions about characters, plot, themes, setting, and important events.
Why Study the Prescribed Text?

items: It carries a significant portion of marks in the Use of English paper.
It tests your ability to analyze literature, a skill useful for university studies.
It rewards thorough reading and understanding of the text.

blocks.text: Make sure you have a copy of the prescribed text and read it at least twice. Take notes on key characters, themes, and events. This section is not about guessing; it's about knowledge of the text.

lessons.title: Chapter / Section Summaries
lessons.summary: How to summarize chapters and sections of the prescribed text for revision.

blocks.text: Creating summaries of each chapter or section is an effective way to revise the prescribed text. A summary should condense the main events and key points of that section without unnecessary detail. This helps you recall the sequence of events and important details.
How to Write a Chapter Summary

items: Read the chapter carefully.
Identify the main events that occur.
Note any new characters introduced or significant character development.
Identify any major revelations or turning points.
Write a concise paragraph covering these points in your own words.

blocks.text: Since the prescribed text varies by year, you should create your own summaries based on the specific novel, play, or book assigned by JAMB. This lesson provides a framework.

lessons.title: Characters
lessons.summary: A guide to analyzing the main characters in the prescribed text.

blocks.text: You should be familiar with the main characters in the prescribed text. For each character, know their role in the plot, their relationships with others, and their key traits. JAMB may ask questions about character motivation, development, or significance.
Character Analysis Framework

items: Name and role in the story.
Physical and personality traits.
Motivations and goals.
Relationships with other characters.
Key actions and their consequences.
Character development (how they change).

blocks.text: Apply this framework to the characters in your prescribed text. Make a list of all important characters and their details.

lessons.title: Character Relationships
lessons.summary: Understanding the relationships between characters and their significance.

blocks.text: Relationships between characters drive the plot and reveal themes. Understanding who is allied with whom, who is in conflict, and how relationships evolve is crucial.
Types of Relationships

items: Familial: parents, siblings, children.
Romantic: couples, lovers.
Friendships: allies, companions.
Antagonistic: rivals, enemies.
Professional: employer-employee, teacher-student.

blocks.text: Practice Question (Generic) In the prescribed text, which character serves as a mentor to the protagonist? (Answer based on your reading.)
Refer to the specific text to answer this. Look for a character who guides or advises the main character.

lessons.title: Setting
lessons.summary: Analyzing the time and place of the prescribed text and its impact.

blocks.text: Setting includes the time period, geographical location, and social environment in which the story takes place. It can influence characters, plot, and themes.
Aspects of Setting

items: Time: Historical period, season, time of day.
Place: Country, city, specific locations (e.g., village, house, school).
Social Context: Cultural norms, political climate, economic conditions.

blocks.text: Practice Question How does the setting of the prescribed text influence the plot? (Answer based on your reading.)
Consider how the time and place create conflict, limit characters' options, or provide opportunities.

lessons.title: Plot
lessons.summary: Understanding the sequence of events and structure of the prescribed text.

blocks.text: The plot is the sequence of events in a story. It typically follows a structure: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution. Understanding the plot helps you answer questions about cause and effect and the overall arc.
Plot Elements

items: Exposition: Introduction of characters, setting, and initial situation.
Rising Action: Events that build tension and lead to the climax.
Climax: The turning point or peak of conflict.
Falling Action: Events after the climax that lead to resolution.
Resolution: The conclusion where conflicts are resolved.

blocks.text: Practice Question What event marks the climax of the prescribed text? (Answer based on your reading.)
Identify the moment of highest tension or the turning point in the story.

lessons.title: Themes
lessons.summary: Identifying and analyzing the major themes of the prescribed text.

blocks.text: Themes are the underlying ideas or messages that the author explores. They are universal concepts such as love, justice, betrayal, identity, freedom, or tradition vs. modernity. JAMB often asks questions about themes.
How to Identify Themes

items: Look at the main conflicts in the story.
Consider the characters' journeys and what they learn.
Examine repeated symbols or motifs.
Think about the author's message or the lesson of the story.

blocks.text: Practice Question What is a major theme in the prescribed text? (Answer based on your reading.)
Provide a theme and explain how it is developed in the text with examples.

lessons.title: Important Events
lessons.summary: Key events in the prescribed text and their significance.

blocks.text: Certain events are pivotal to the plot and themes. You should be able to identify and explain the significance of these events.
Examples of Important Events

items: A character's death or birth.
A major decision or turning point.
A revelation or discovery.
A conflict or confrontation.
A journey or change of setting.

blocks.text: Practice Question What is the significance of the event where the protagonist leaves his hometown? (Answer based on your reading.)
Explain how this event affects the character and the plot.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.summary: Important vocabulary words from the prescribed text and their meanings.

blocks.text: The prescribed text may contain challenging vocabulary. You should make a list of unfamiliar words, look up their meanings, and understand their usage in context. JAMB may test vocabulary directly from the text.
How to Build Vocabulary

items: Read with a dictionary.
Write down new words and definitions.
Review the list regularly.
Try to use the words in sentences.

blocks.text: Since the text varies, you must identify and learn the vocabulary yourself.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.summary: In-depth analysis of main characters, including their development and role.

blocks.text: Beyond basic character identification, you may need to analyze a character's development, motivations, and significance to the story. Be prepared to write about how a character changes or what they represent.
Analysis Questions

items: How does the character evolve over the course of the text?
What is the character's primary motivation?
How does the character contribute to the themes?
What is the character's role in the plot (protagonist, antagonist, foil)?

lessons.title: Theme Questions
lessons.summary: Practice questions focusing on themes from the prescribed text.

blocks.text: Here are some generic theme-based questions. You should apply them to your specific text.
1. How does the author explore the theme of injustice in the text?
2. What does the text say about the importance of family?
3. How is the theme of tradition versus modernity presented?
Answers will vary depending on the text. Use your knowledge of the text to provide specific examples and explanations.

lessons.title: Event Questions
lessons.summary: Practice questions focusing on key events in the prescribed text.

blocks.text: Here are some generic event-based questions.
1. What event leads to the protagonist's change in attitude?
2. How does the conflict between Character A and Character B escalate?
3. What is the outcome of the main conflict?
Provide specific details from the text.

lessons.title: Full Reading Text Revision
lessons.summary: A summary of how to revise the prescribed text effectively.

blocks.text: To revise the prescribed text, focus on the following key areas:

items: Main characters and their traits.
Plot summary and key events.
Major themes and how they are developed.
Setting and its significance.
Important quotations or dialogues.
Relationships between characters.

blocks.text: Create a revision sheet with these points. Practice writing short answers to potential questions.

lessons.title: JAMB-Style Reading Text Questions
lessons.summary: Sample JAMB-style questions on the prescribed text (generic framework).

blocks.text: Here are examples of the types of questions you might see. Since the text is unknown, use these to practice your analysis skills.
1. The character of X is best described as... A. cruel B. kind C. ambitious D. naive
2. The author uses the setting to... A. create mood B. advance the plot C. symbolize isolation D. all of the above
3. The main conflict in the text is between... A. X and Y B. tradition and change C. love and duty D. individual and society
Answers will depend on the actual prescribed text. Use this as practice to analyze any text critically.
